Chapter 1

Sanjaya said: 
Having spoken thus, 
Gudakesha (Arjuna, the conqueror of sleep), 
the son of Kunti, 
drew up his excellent chariot 
in the midst of the two armies, 
facing Bhishma, Drona, 
and all the other kings, 
and said to the son of Pritha (Arjuna), 
"Behold these assembled Kurus."

Commentary: 
The word 'Gudakesha' has two meanings: 
(1) 'Guda' means curly and 'Kesha' means hair. One whose hair is curly is called 'Gudakesha'. (2) 'Guda' means sleep and 'Isha' means lord. One who is the lord of sleep, i.e., one who has control over sleep, 
is called 'Gudakesha'. Arjuna's hair was curly, and he had control over sleep; 
hence he is called 'Gudakesha'. When the Lord's devotee, who is not a slave to the pleasure of sleep and laziness, 
and who is not a servant of sensual pleasures, 
speaks, the Lord listens to him; 
not only does He listen, but He also obeys his command. Therefore, when his friend and devotee Arjuna gave the order, 
the omniscient Lord Sri Krishna drew up Arjuna's chariot 
in the midst of the two armies. The word 'Kuru' includes both the sons of Dhritarashtra and the sons of Pandu, 
as both are of the Kuru dynasty. The purpose of saying "Behold these assembled Kurus" 
is to make Arjuna realize that all of them are his own kin, 
whether they are on his side or on the opposing side, 
whether they are good or bad, virtuous or wicked. This will awaken Arjuna's dormant family affection and attachment, 
and he will become inquisitive, 
which will provide an opportunity for the Lord to impart the great teachings of the Gita 
for the benefit of future beings in the Kali Yuga. If the Lord had said, "Behold these assembled Dhritarashtras," 
it would have aroused Arjuna's desire to fight, 
and the opportunity for the Gita to be revealed would not have arisen. Moreover, Arjuna's dormant family attachment would not have been removed, 
which the Lord considers His own responsibility. Just as a doctor first tries to ripen a boil and then cuts it open to clean it, 
the Lord first awakens the dormant attachment in His devotee 
and then removes it. Here, the Lord is awakening Arjuna's dormant attachment by saying "Behold these Kurus," 
which He will later remove through His teachings. The Lord drew up Arjuna's chariot in a place where Arjuna could see 
his relatives, including Bhishma, Drona, and other kings. The Lord did not need to say "Behold" (pashya), 
as He could have simply drawn up the chariot. However, the Lord said "pashya" to indicate that He was obeying Arjuna's command. The word 'Hrishikesha' means the lord of the senses. The Lord, who is the controller of the mind, intellect, and senses, 
has become obedient to Arjuna's command. This shows the Lord's great mercy towards Arjuna. The Lord drew up Arjuna's excellent chariot in the midst of the two armies, 
in the empty space between them.

english:
Chapter 1, Verses 26-28

The Lord, having placed the chariot in the middle, said to Arjun, "Behold these Kurus." The Lord's intention was to awaken Arjun from his illusion. In familial affection, there is attachment and a sense of ownership, whereas in devotion to the Lord, there is a sense of intimacy and selflessness. Familial affection is characterized by ignorance and darkness, while devotion to the Lord is marked by knowledge and illumination. In familial affection, one becomes neglectful of their duty, whereas in devotion to the Lord, one may forget their worldly duties, but the devotee never forsakes their duty. There is a significant difference between familial affection and devotion to the Lord. When one is attached to their family, they tend to overlook their family members' faults, thinking, "They are mine." Similarly, when one is devoted to the Lord, they tend to overlook the faults of other devotees, thinking, "They are mine." However, in devotion to the Lord, the Lord's supremacy is paramount. Now, having said this, Sanjay will describe what happened next. Arjun, the son of Pritha, saw his fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, and well-wishers, as well as his fathers-in-law and friends, standing in both armies. (Verse 26)

He saw them standing in their respective positions, ready for battle. Among them were Bhishma, Drona, and other elders, as well as his own sons, such as Abhimanyu, and the sons of his brothers, like Lakshmana. He also saw his friends, such as Sathyaki and Kritavarma, standing in the enemy's army. Having seen all his relatives standing in their positions, Arjun, the son of Kunti, was overcome with compassion and sorrow. With a heavy heart, he spoke the following words: (Verse 27)

## Chapter 1

Having seen these relatives standing before him, Arjuna, the son of Kunti, was overcome with great compassion (kripaya). The words "sa kaunteyah" imply that Arjuna, who was sent to the battlefield by his mother Kunti and had asked Lord Krishna to position the chariot between the two armies so that he could see the main warriors, was now filled with extreme cowardice. Upon seeing his relatives on both sides, Arjuna thought that whether the people on this side or that side die, the loss would be his own, and his family would be destroyed. This thought led to the disappearance of his desire to fight and the emergence of cowardice within him. This cowardice is referred to by Lord Krishna as "kashmalam" and "hridayadaurbalyam" (2.2-3), and Arjuna himself acknowledges it as "karpanyakoshopahatasvabhavah" (2.7). The fact that Arjuna is now overcome with compassion (kripaya) indicates that this cowardice was not present earlier but has arisen now. As it is a newly acquired flaw, it will not persist. On the other hand, Arjuna's natural bravery will endure. Extreme cowardice refers to the absence of any desire to kill or harm those who are bent on causing harm, such as Duryodhana, Dushasana, and Shakuni, despite being faced with the opportunity to do so. In Arjuna's case, he has been overcome by such cowardice that he feels compassion even for those who are wicked and wish him harm. Arjuna said:
Upon seeing these relatives of mine, who are eager to fight, O Krishna, my limbs weaken, and my mouth dries up. My body trembles, and my hair stands on end. (28)
My Gandiva bow slips from my hand, and my skin burns. I am unable to stand steady, and my mind is bewildered. (29-30)

In my body, my limbs are weakening, and my mouth is drying up. My body is trembling, and my hair is standing on end.

Chapter 1, Verse 31:
My hands are releasing the bow, Gandiva, and my skin is burning; I am unable to stand steady, and my mind is bewildered, as if it is on fire. Commentary: The term "Krsna" is very dear to Arjuna, and it appears nine times in the Gita. Similarly, the term "Partha" is very dear to Lord Krsna. They used to address each other by these names, and this was well-known to the people. Hence, Sanjaya mentions these names at the end of the Gita: "Where there is Krsna, the Lord of Yoga, and where there is Partha, the wielder of the bow" (18.78). Dhrtarastra had previously said "samaveta yuyutsavah" (assembled for battle), and Arjuna says "yuyutsam samupasthitam" (assembled for battle). However, there is a significant difference in their perspectives. Dhrtarastra sees a distinction between his sons (the Kauravas) and the sons of Pandu (the Pandavas), whereas Arjuna does not see this distinction. Hence, Arjuna uses the term "svajanam" (my own people), which includes both parties. The commentary explains that Arjuna's mind is filled with anxiety and sorrow as he contemplates the impending battle. His body is experiencing various symptoms, such as numbness in his hands and feet, dryness in his mouth, and trembling of his entire body. His skin is burning, and his mind is bewildered. He is unable to stand steady, and his famous bow, Gandiva, is slipping from his hands. The commentary also quotes a verse that compares anxiety (cintā) to a funeral pyre (citā), stating that anxiety burns the living, while the funeral pyre burns the dead. Arjuna says: I see adverse omens, O Krsna, and I do not foresee any good in killing my own people in this battle. (31)

## Chapter 1, Verse 50
Oh Keshav, I see inauspicious omens (nimittani), and having killed my own people (svajanam), I do not see any benefit (shreyah) in this war. The Hindi commentary explains that Arjun is seeing both the omens and the consequences of the war as inauspicious. He is saying that he does not see any benefit in killing his own people, and that this war will not bring any good to him or his family, either in this world or the next. The reason is that the person who destroys his own family is considered a great sinner and will suffer in hell. The commentary further explains that the omens Arjun is seeing are not just external signs, but also his own physical and mental state. His body is weakening, his mind is filled with doubt, and he is experiencing other bad omens. All these signs are indicating that the war will not be beneficial for him. ## Verse 32
Oh Krishna, I do not desire victory (vijayam), nor do I desire a kingdom (rajyam) or pleasures (sukhani). Oh Govind, what is the use of a kingdom (kim no rajyena) or pleasures (kim bhogaih) or even life (jiviten va) to us? In this verse, Arjun is expressing his disillusionment with the idea of war and the desire for victory, kingdom, or pleasures. He is asking Krishna what is the point of all these things if they come at the cost of killing his own people and suffering in the process. The commentary explains that Arjun is not just talking about the external omens, but also about his own internal state. He is saying that even if they win the war, it will not bring them any real benefit or happiness. The commentary also notes that the omens and signs that Arjun is seeing are not just random events, but are actually indicative of the future consequences of their actions.

Shloka 33-34]

* The Seeker - The Reviver *

Explanation: 
Let us assume that we win the war, then victory would lead to our kingdom on the entire earth, and we would have authority. With the kingdom, we would get various kinds of happiness. However, I do not desire any of these, i.e., my mind does not have any desire for victory, kingdom, and happiness. 'Kinn no rajyena Govinda, kinn bhojair jeevitena va' - 
If we do not have any desire for victory, kingdom, and happiness, then why do we need a big kingdom? Why do we need any kind of enjoyment? Even if we get many beautiful things to enjoy, what benefit will we get from them? Or, even if we live for many years, enjoying the happiness of the kingdom, what benefit will we get from it? The implication is that victory, kingdom, and enjoyment can only bring happiness when there is a desire for them, when they are cherished, and when they are valued. However, we do not have any desire for them. Therefore, what happiness can they bring to us? We do not have any desire to live by killing our relatives; because when our relatives die, what will the kingdom and enjoyment be for? Explanation: 
The kingdom, enjoyment, etc., are meant for the family. But when the family itself dies, who will enjoy them? It is not a question of enjoying them; on the contrary, we will have more worries and grief. Relation: 
Arjuna does not want victory, etc., for himself. The reason for this is explained in the next shloka. Shloka 33]
Those for whom we desire victory, kingdom, and happiness, they are the ones who are standing in the battlefield, giving up their lives and wealth. Explanation: 
We do not have any attachment to our life and wealth; we do not have any greed for them. We want victory, kingdom, and happiness for our relatives, friends, etc. We want them to be happy, to be comfortable, to be served, and to be pleased. This is why we want to fight and win the kingdom, to gather wealth, etc. 'Theyamre vsthita yuddhe pranans tyaktva dhanan cha' - 
But those very people, who are standing in the battlefield, giving up their lives and wealth, have made up their minds that they will fight, even if they die. If they die, then what is the use of the kingdom, happiness, and wealth to us? What is the use of them for us? Explanation: 
The phrase 'pranans tyaktva dhanan cha' means that they have given up their attachment to their life and wealth. They have given up their desire to live and their attachment to wealth. If they had any attachment to their life and wealth, they would not have come to fight in the battlefield. Therefore, this phrase means that they have given up their attachment to their life and wealth. Relation: 
Those for whom we want victory, kingdom, and happiness, they are our relatives, friends, etc. This is explained by Arjuna in the next two shlokas. Shloka 34]
Gurus, fathers, sons, and grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives. Explanation: 
We want victory, kingdom, and happiness for our gurus, fathers, sons, grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives.

Chapter 1, Verse 35:
I do not wish to kill them, even if I were to attain the dominion of the three worlds, O Madhusudana (killer of the demon Madhu). What to speak of the earth? Commentary:
"'Acharyah pitarah kim nu mahikrite' - If my relatives, including my teachers, fathers, and grandfathers, were to attack me out of anger to destroy me, even then I do not wish to kill them. If they were to attack me out of greed for the kingdom, even then I do not wish to kill them out of greed for the kingdom. In other words, I do not wish to kill them, even if it means attaining the kingdom of the earth. The use of the word 'api' twice implies that Arjuna means to say that even if his relatives were to attack him first, he would not wish to kill them. Even if they were to attack him out of a desire to destroy him, he would not wish to kill them. And even if killing them would result in his attaining the kingdom of the three worlds, he would not wish to kill them. The address 'Madhusudana' implies that Lord Krishna is the slayer of demons, but these relatives of mine, including Drona and Bhishma, are not demons. They are our close relatives, and I do not wish to kill them. The word 'Acharyah' refers to the teachers, including Drona, who are the most revered and worthy of respect. The fact that Arjuna mentions them first, before his fathers and grandfathers, indicates that he is considering the fact that they are his spiritual guides and benefactors."

english:
Chapter 1, Verse 36:
Having killed the sons of Dhritarashtra, O Janardana, what pleasure would we get? Killing these aggressors would lead to sin only. Commentary:
In the previous verse, Arjuna mentioned two reasons for not killing his relatives. Now, he explains that even from the perspective of consequences, killing his relatives is not justified. If we consider our relationship with our teachers, it is one of knowledge and benefit. We should wish for their happiness, comfort, and service. Should we serve them or fight with them? We should surrender ourselves, our lives, to the feet of our teachers. This is what is proper for us. Our ancestors (pitarah) are related to our body, and our body is a manifestation of them. How can we, driven by anger or greed, kill our own ancestors? Our maternal uncles (matulah) are the brothers of our mothers, who nourished and raised us. Therefore, they are also worthy of reverence, just like our mothers. Our fathers-in-law (shvashurah) are the revered fathers of our wives and the brothers of our mothers. Hence, they are equivalent to our own fathers. How can we kill them? Our grandsons (pautrah) are even more deserving of nourishment and care than our sons. Our husbands' brothers, our brothers-in-law (shyalah), are the beloved brothers of our wives. Our sons (putrah) and our brothers' sons are completely dependent on us for their care and upbringing. Even if they act against us, it is our duty (dharma) to care for them. Our grandfathers (pitamahah) and other relatives are also worthy of reverence and care. We should serve them and ensure their well-being, rather than killing them. Even if we were to gain dominion over the three worlds, it would not be justified to kill them. On the contrary, our efforts should be directed towards ensuring their happiness and comfort, so that they may not suffer in any way. Arjuna says that killing his relatives, the sons of Dhritarashtra, who are aggressors, would not bring him any joy. Instead, it would lead to sin, and in this world, he would never experience happiness. The sin incurred by killing them would also lead to terrible suffering in the afterlife. There are six types of aggressors: those who set fires, those who administer poison, those who are armed and ready to kill, those who steal wealth, those who seize land, and those who abduct women. Duryodhana and his allies exhibited all these characteristics. They had tried to burn the Pandavas alive in the lacquer house and had also attempted to kill Bhima by feeding him poison. If we were to kill all the soldiers and emerge victorious, would we experience any joy? If, driven by anger or greed, we were to kill our relatives, we would later regret our actions and lament what we had done. The memory of our slain relatives would haunt us, and we would be constantly afflicted by grief. In such a state, how could we ever experience happiness?

Chapter 1, Verse 37
Therefore, we are not worthy of killing our own relatives, the sons of Dhritarashtra. How can we be happy after killing our own people, O Madhava? Commentary: 'Therefore, we are not worthy of killing our own relatives, the sons of Dhritarashtra' - Up to this point (from the twenty-eighth verse of the first chapter to here), I have presented many arguments and considerations for not killing our relatives. Given these, how can we engage in such an unrighteous act? It is entirely unsuitable for us to kill our own relatives, the sons of Dhritarashtra. How can we, who are considered good people, perform such an unsuitable act? 'How can we be happy after killing our own people, O Madhava?' - We are already experiencing sorrow and distress, and if we kill them in a fit of rage and greed, our sorrow will only increase. How can we be happy after killing our own relatives? Here, Arjuna's vision is obscured by his affection and attachment to his relatives, and he is unable to see his duty as a Kshatriya. When there is attachment, a person's discernment is clouded, and their attachment grows stronger. As attachment grows, one loses sight of their duty. It is stated in the Arthashastra that one should kill an aggressor, while the Dharmashastra teaches that one should not harm anyone. Arthashastra is concerned with self-interest, whereas Dharmashastra is concerned with righteousness, without any self-interest. Dharmashastra takes precedence over Arthashastra. Therefore, when there is a conflict between Arthashastra and Dharmashastra, one should abandon Arthashastra and follow Dharmashastra. As stated in the Yajnavalkya Smriti: "In the event of a conflict between the two, the Dharmashastra is considered more authoritative, as it is based on righteousness and is more powerful in practice." (Yajnavalkya Smriti 2.21)

Chapter 1, Verses 38-39]

Although these people, with their minds corrupted by greed, do not see the fault in the destruction of their family (kula-kshaya) and the sin of violating friendship (mitra-droha), 
we should know how to refrain from sin, O Janardana, for we see the destruction of our family and the sin of violating friendship. (38-39)

Commentary: 
Now, a doubt arises here that just as Duryodhana and others are your relatives, you are also their relative. You are thinking of retreating from the war from the perspective of your relatives, but Duryodhana and others are not thinking of retreating from the war. What is the reason for this? Arjuna answers this question in the next two verses. Although these people, with their minds corrupted by greed, do not see the fault in the destruction of their family and the sin of violating friendship, we should know how to refrain from sin, O Janardana, for we see the destruction of our family and the sin of violating friendship. The term "lobha" refers to the tendency of the mind to constantly crave for more wealth, land, houses, respect, praise, position, and power. Due to this tendency, the power of discernment (viveka) is lost, and they do not consider that the kingdom for which they are prepared to commit such a great sin and destroy their family will not remain with them forever. They do not think about what will happen to them when the kingdom is lost, and what will happen to the kingdom when they are gone. When a person enjoys the pleasure of union, they must also endure the pain of separation. The pain of separation is greater than the pleasure of union. The point is that due to the dominance of greed in their minds, they only see the kingdom and do not consider the destruction of their family and the sin of violating friendship. Wherever there is war, there is destruction of time, wealth, and power, and various anxieties and calamities arise. We are living comfortably even without the things we currently lack. However, when we acquire these things and then lose them, we experience great sorrow. The point is that the constant lack of these things was not as painful as the sorrow of losing them after acquiring them. In the case of friendship, even a small dispute can lead to malice and enmity. For example, Drupada and Drona were childhood friends, but Drupada humiliated Drona when he received a kingdom. This led to enmity between them, and Drona took revenge by defeating Drupada and taking half of his kingdom. Drupada then performed a sacrifice to destroy Drona, which resulted in the birth of Dhristadyumna and Draupadi. This shows how enmity can arise even among friends, leading to great sin. These people, however, do not consider this and are only thinking of acquiring more wealth and power.

english:
Chapter 1, Verse 40
When the family is destroyed, the eternal family traditions (kula dharma) are destroyed. When these traditions are destroyed, the entire family is overcome by sin (adharma). In the commentary, it is explained that when a person is attached to worldly possessions, they experience suffering due to separation from them. Despite this, humans continue to strive for things they lack, driven by greed (lobha). Upon reflection, it becomes clear that even if these things are acquired, they will eventually be lost. Thus, our situation remains the same as it was before acquiring them. The effort to acquire them only leads to suffering, and any fleeting happiness is a result of greed. If there were no greed, there would be no happiness in acquiring things. Similarly, without the flaw of attachment (moha), there can be no happiness in family relationships, and without the flaw of covetousness (lalcha), there can be no happiness in accumulating wealth. The point is that worldly happiness is always rooted in some flaw. Without flaws, there can be no worldly happiness. However, due to greed, humans are unable to consider this. The commentary further explains that even if friends cause us suffering, it is not harmful to us, as it can lead to the destruction of our past sins and purification. However, if we harbor hatred or enmity towards them, it will remain with us even after death and prompt us to commit sins, leading to our downfall. We should consider avoiding this sinful behavior. Arjuna's gaze is fixed on the greed of Duryodhana and others, but he himself is bound by familial affection (moha) and fails to recognize his own duty. This is a common phenomenon, where people focus on the flaws of others and fail to see their own. As long as one's attention is on the flaws of others, they will not recognize their own flaws and will instead develop a sense of pride, thinking they are flawless. Arjuna, too, sees the flaws in Duryodhana and others, but not his own, and thus fails to understand his duty. Arjuna says that even if Duryodhana and others do not see the flaws in their actions, we should still consider the consequences of destroying our family and the sins that come with it. We are aware of the flaws that arise from destroying our family, and we should reflect on them. The flaws that arise from destroying our family are described in the following verses. In Verse 40, it is stated that when the family is destroyed, the eternal family traditions are destroyed, and when these traditions are destroyed, the entire family is overcome by sin.

Commentary - 'Kulakshaye Pranashyanti' - Sadhaka Sanjivani, Page 57
When the family duty (kula dharma) is not performed, and the undesired actions are performed, it leads to the downfall of the entire family, i.e., the entire family is filled with unrighteousness (adharma). 'Sanatana' - when war occurs, it leads to the decline of the family (vansa). Since the beginning of the family, the righteous duties (kula dharma) of the family, the pure traditions, and the noble customs have been followed. However, when the family is destroyed, what will remain to be affected by unrighteousness? The answer is that the men who are capable of fighting will be killed in the war, but the children and women who are not capable of fighting will remain. They will be affected by unrighteousness because, when the knowledgeable and experienced men who know the scriptures and customs are killed, the remaining people will not receive proper guidance. As a result, they will act according to their whims, leading to the decline of noble conduct and righteous behavior. When the family's righteous duties (kula dharma) are destroyed, the entire family is filled with unrighteousness. This is because, when the family's noble traditions and customs are lost, the people will act without knowledge, leading to the performance of undesired actions and the non-performance of desired actions. Therefore, unrighteousness will prevail. Verse 41:
Adharma-abhibhavat Krsna pradusyanti kulastriyah,
Strisu dustasu Varsneya jayate varnasankarah. Oh Krsna, when unrighteousness (adharma) prevails, the women of the family become corrupted. Oh Varsneya, when the women become corrupted, the offspring will be of mixed caste (varna-sankara). Commentary - 'Adharma-abhibhavat Krsna pradusyanti kulastriyah' - When righteous behavior (dharma) is followed, the heart becomes pure. A pure heart leads to a sattviki (pure) intellect, which possesses the ability to discern right from wrong. However, when unrighteousness (adharma) prevails in the family, the conduct becomes impure, leading to an impure heart. An impure heart leads to a tamasi (dark) intellect, causing the individual to consider undesired actions as desired and vice versa. This, in turn, leads to the corruption of the women of the family, making them unchaste. 'Strisu dustasu Varsneya jayate varnasankarah' - When the women become corrupted, the offspring will be of mixed caste (varna-sankara). When a man and a woman of different castes (varna) have a child, the child is considered to be of mixed caste (varna-sankara). Arjuna addresses Krsna as 'Krsna' (the one who attracts all) and asks Him to guide their family. He also addresses Krsna as 'Varsneya' (the descendant of Vrsni), implying that if their family is destroyed, who will remain to be considered a descendant of Vrsni? The term 'varna-sankara' refers to the mixture of two opposing righteous duties (dharma), resulting in a corrupted state. When righteous duties are not followed, various types of corruption occur, including dharma-sankara (corruption of righteous duties), varna-sankara (corruption of castes), jati-sankara (corruption of species), kula-sankara (corruption of family), vesa-sankara (corruption of attire), bhasa-sankara (corruption of language), and ahara-sankara (corruption of food).

english:
Chapter 1, Verse 42:
The mixture (of castes) leads to hell for both the family destroyers and the family itself. The ancestors of these (family destroyers) also fall (from their position) due to the loss of offerings of food and water (pinda and udaka). Explanation - When the ancestors receive offerings of food and water, they reside in higher realms due to the influence of merit. However, when these offerings cease, they fall from their position. The reason for this is that the mixed-caste offspring lack the wisdom to perform these offerings, as they are born without adherence to traditional norms. They do not follow the family duties (kula dharma) and instead act contrary to them. Those who have destroyed their family through war are called "kula ghata" (family destroyers). The mixture of castes leads these family destroyers and their entire family to hell. The ancestors of these family destroyers do not receive offerings of food and water due to the lack of reverence and adherence to tradition in their mixed-caste offspring. Even if these offspring perform offerings, they are not done according to traditional norms, and therefore, the ancestors do not receive them. As a result, the ancestors fall from their position. Chapter 1, Verse 43:
These faults, which are the causes of the mixture of castes and are found in family destroyers, destroy the eternal duties of caste (jati dharma) and family (kula dharma). Explanation - The mixture of castes, resulting from the faults of family destroyers, leads to the destruction of the traditional duties of both caste and family, which have been in place since ancient times. When a family is destroyed in war, the traditional duties of the family, which are passed down through generations, are also destroyed. This, in turn, leads to the destruction of the duties of the caste, as the family's traditional norms are lost. As a result, the family becomes increasingly immersed in immorality, and the women of the family become corrupted, leading to the birth of mixed-caste offspring. What are kula dharma and jati dharma? They refer to the separate traditions and norms that exist within a single caste, distinguishing one family from another.

english:
Shloka 44-45

There are different social norms and different ways of conduct, which are all known as 'varṇa-dharma' or 'jāti-dharma', which are a part of the general 'dharma' or righteous duty. All these 'jāti-dharmas' are complete and are determined by the scriptures. The dharma that is followed by the community and the family is also known as 'kul-dharma'. If these kul-dharmas are not followed, then these dharmas are destroyed. O Janārdana! We have heard that the people whose kul-dharma is destroyed, their residence in this world is hell. (atman, dharma)

The residence of humans is hell, for a long time, we have heard. (atman, dharma)

Commentary:

The Lord has given man the power of discrimination and the authority to perform new actions. Therefore, he is free to perform or not perform actions, to do good or bad, and to act wisely or foolishly. Therefore, he should always perform his duties with discrimination and wisdom. But man, due to his attachment to worldly pleasures and desires, disregards his discrimination and becomes a slave to his passions and hatred. As a result, his conduct becomes contrary to the scriptures and the norms of his family. As a result, he is criticized and humiliated in this world and suffers in hell in the next world. We have heard this from our elders. The word 'manuṣyaṇām' includes all humans, including those who have committed sins in the past, his own self, and those who will come in the future. Relation: The effect of the description of the evil consequences of the war on Arjuna is described in the next shloka. We have decided to commit a great sin. We are ready to kill our relatives due to our attachment to the pleasures of the kingdom and the kingdom itself. (atman, dharma)

Commentary: 'Ahō bat...' - It is a great wonder and a great sin that we have decided to commit. These people are wicked and have no regard for dharma. They are under the influence of their passions and hatred. Therefore, it is not surprising that they are ready to fight. But we are aware of what is right and wrong, we know what is dharma and adharma, what is good and bad. Despite this knowledge, we are acting like ignorant people. Not only that, we are ready to fight with our own relatives, armed with weapons. This is a great wonder and a great sin for us. Note: The word 'anuśhuśrūm' is used by Arjuna in a reflexive way, indicating that he is shocked and saddened by the situation.

*
The Bhagavad Gita
*

[Chapter 1
We have received education from our gurus, and we have thought about how to improve our lives. But we have not considered the respect due to them. We have thought about committing a great sin (papam) by engaging in war - this is a very heavy sin (mahat-papam). ]

The words "ah" and "bat" have appeared in this shloka. The word "ah" is an expression of wonder. The wonder is that we have decided to commit a great sin (papam) of war, knowing that it will lead to a series of unfortunate events. The word "bat" is an expression of sorrow and grief. The sorrow is that we are ready to kill our own family members due to our attachment to a short-lived kingdom and fleeting pleasures. The reason for committing a great sin (papam) and being ready to kill our own family members is solely due to our attachment to a kingdom and pleasures. If we win the war, we will get a kingdom, wealth, and respect, and our influence will spread throughout the kingdom. We will be able to get whatever we want, and we will be able to live a life of luxury and pleasure. This is the reason why we are ready to commit a great sin (papam). But if we are victorious in the war, who can stop us from committing further evil deeds? No one can stop us. Here, Arjuna's attention is focused on the act of war. He wants to avoid war because he considers it to be a wrong action. But he has not considered what the real fault is. The fault is not in the act of war itself, but in the attachment to a kingdom and pleasures. Due to this attachment, he is expressing wonder and sorrow, which is not suitable for a wise, righteous, and brave warrior. [Arjuna had earlier (in the 38th shloka) mentioned that the fault of the war is due to the attachment to a kingdom and pleasures. He is now saying that he is ready to commit a great sin (papam) due to his attachment to a kingdom and pleasures. This shows that Arjuna considers attachment to be the cause of sin (papam). But later (in the 36th shloka of the third chapter), Arjuna asks why a person commits a wrong action even when he does not want to. The answer is that he is not considering the higher perspective, but is only looking at the physical body and the worldly life. Therefore, he is considering attachment to be the cause of sin (papam).]

Relation - Arjuna, who is filled with wonder and sorrow, will now explain his final conclusion in the next shloka. If I were to be unarmed and facing the enemy with their weapons, 
the Dhartarashtras would kill me in the battle. It would be better for me to be unarmed.

In reality, the Lord did not make Arjuna fight, but rather imparted knowledge of his duty to him. The war was already a duty that Arjuna had to fulfill. Therefore, the thought of war was Arjuna's own, and he himself was inclined to fight; it was only then that he brought the Lord to the battlefield. However, Arjuna, recognizing that this thought of his would lead to his downfall, was hesitant to fight, i.e., he was abandoning his duty. On this, the Lord said, "This reluctance of yours to fight is due to your attachment." Therefore, it is not proper to abandon the duty that has been obtained at the right time. Explanation—Arjuna says, "If I were to renounce the war, would it not be for my own good?" The Lord's greatness is such that if Arjuna were to renounce the war completely, the people of the world, who are bound by worldly considerations, would think that Arjuna has renounced the war for his own good. They would not understand the Lord's words, and they would think that Arjuna is renouncing the war because he is afraid of it. But, Arjuna, being a warrior, would not be able to renounce the war, and the people would think that he is renouncing the war because he is a coward. Therefore, Arjuna's renunciation of the war would be considered a sin. Arjuna thought, "If I were to renounce the war, it would be for my own good, and I would be able to avoid the sin of killing my relatives. If I were to renounce the war, I would be able to avoid the sin of killing my relatives, and my family would not be destroyed." Up to now, Arjuna has been saying that he is a righteous person and that he will not fight in the war. 62

Here, Arjuna has arrived. Therefore, even without fighting this war, the opposition (of the Kauravas) would not have been defeated. My five sons, including Bhishma, and Abhimanyu would not have been saved (from death). There were many reasons for this war, and it was inevitable. It would have happened even if Arjuna had not fought. If Arjuna had not fought, Yudhishthira, Arjuna's brother, would have fought the war at his mother's behest. Bhima, Arjuna's brother, would not have retreated from the war, as he had vowed to kill the Kauravas. Droupadi had said that if her husband (the Pandavas) did not fight the Kauravas, her father (Droupadi's father, Drupad) would be disowned by her. There were many such reasons, making it impossible to avoid the war. It is not in the power of a human to stop something that is destined to happen. However, by performing one's duty, a human can attain liberation and avoid destruction. This means that a human is free to choose between right and wrong. Therefore, the Lord has imparted knowledge of duty to Arjuna, teaching him that he should be prepared to perform his duty in accordance with the scriptures. Sanjaya said:

Thus, after speaking to Arjuna, he sat down on his chariot in the battlefield, surrounded by his charioteer, with his bow and arrow in hand, his mind overcome with grief. (47)

After speaking thus, Arjuna sat down on his chariot in the battlefield, surrounded by his charioteer, with his bow and arrow in hand, his mind overcome with grief, having discarded his quiver. The Lord's words to Arjuna, urging him to fight and the Kauravas, and Arjuna's inner turmoil, are the root of all evil. The Lord's words to Arjuna, urging him to fight, have awakened Arjuna's attachment, and he says that in the war, his relatives will be killed, and he will go to hell in the afterlife. Arjuna, overcome with anxiety, has made up his mind not to fight. The Kauravas, led by Duryodhana, have been driven by greed, and they have come to this battlefield, not looking at the Lord, who is standing in front of them, with his bow and arrow in hand. However, Arjuna, with a troubled mind, has come to this battlefield, where the Kauravas have come, armed with their bows and arrows, and has sat down in a state of grief, having discarded his quiver and bow. If Bhima and Arjuna, who are kind and desirous of peace, are killed, and my father, who is old, fights with his five brave sons, the Kauravas will fight with them. (Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 82.37-38)

Chapter 1: Arjuna's Despondency Yoga

47]
* The Nectar of the Seeker *
63
Arjuna's despondency arises because he is overcome by the influence of attachment, and he becomes reluctant to fight. This is the glory of attachment, which makes Arjuna see the benefit in holding onto his bow, even when it might lead to his own death. And yet, it is the same Arjuna who, overcome by attachment, is now about to give up his bow, along with the arrows, and is sitting in sorrow, overcome with grief. Thus, with the utterance of the sacred words "Om, Tat, Sat," the first chapter of the dialogue between Shri Krishna and Arjuna, "Arjuna's Despondency Yoga," comes to an end. 1

The great sage Vyas has written the following verse at the end of each chapter, which reveals the special glory and effect of the Bhagavad Gita. "Om, Tat, Sat" - these three sacred words are the pure names of the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman), which are capable of bringing about the well-being of all living beings. By uttering these words, one is able to face the Supreme Consciousness and purify one's actions and their consequences (Karma). Therefore, the recitation of the Gita's chapters, with the correct pronunciation of the shlokas, words, and letters, is purified by the utterance of "Om, Tat, Sat" at the end of each chapter, in order to remove any defects in the recitation and to bring about a sense of detachment from the world and a remembrance of the Supreme Consciousness. In this Upanishad, the essence of all Upanishads is contained, and it is itself a divine weapon, a Bhagavad-bani. Therefore, it is called an Upanishad. This knowledge of the Supreme Consciousness (Brahmavidya) is the most excellent knowledge that is capable of bringing about the well-being of all living beings, without any attachment to varna, ashram, or sampradaya. In this Gita, the teachings of various yogas, such as karma yoga, jnana yoga, dhyana yoga, and bhakti yoga, are given, which enable the seeker to experience the eternal bond with the Supreme Consciousness. Therefore, it is called a yoga-shastra. This is the dialogue between the Supreme Consciousness (Purushottam) Shri Krishna and the great devotee Arjuna. Arjuna asked questions with an unhesitating spirit, and the Supreme Consciousness answered them with great liberality. The meaning of "Om" is that my creation is free from defects. The meaning of "Tat" is that my creation is established in the Supreme Consciousness. The meaning of "Sat" is that my creation is eternal and gives eternal fruit. The meaning of "Iti" is that this is my intention, and I have no other intention. The Gita is called "Shrimat" because it is the supreme knowledge that is full of all auspicious qualities. It is called "Shrimat" because it is the knowledge that is full of all auspicious qualities, such as wealth, dharma, fame, beauty, knowledge, and detachment. The Supreme Consciousness (Brahman) is always present in all beings, and it is the source of all auspicious qualities. Therefore, it is called "Shrimat" because it is the knowledge that is full of all auspicious qualities. The Gita is called "Gita" because it is the song of the Supreme Consciousness, which is sung in a state of ecstasy and joy. Although the Gita is a masculine noun according to the rules of Sanskrit grammar, it is called "Gita" because it is the song of the Supreme Consciousness. In this first chapter, the description of Arjuna's despondency is given. This despondency is also the cause of the well-being of the world, as it leads to detachment from the world and a remembrance of the Supreme Consciousness. Although Duryodhana and others also experienced despondency, their despondency was not a yoga, as it was not caused by a remembrance of the Supreme Consciousness. Only Arjuna's despondency became a yoga, as it was caused by a remembrance of the Supreme Consciousness. Therefore, this chapter is called "Arjuna's Despondency Yoga."

The purpose of writing the puspika at the end of each chapter is that if the seeker reflects on one chapter thoroughly, his well-being will be achieved through that one chapter alone. * To be seen - Gita - 17th chapter, 23rd to 27th shlokas.

Appendix - In the Gita, the dialogue of Shri Krishna and Arjuna begins and ends in devotion... The three words "Brahmavidyayam", "Yogashastre", and "Shrikrishnarjunsamvad" appear in the singular, while "Shreemad Bhagavad Gitaasu" and "Upanishatsu" appear in the plural. This implies that the Bhagavad Gita is one of the Upanishads, which includes "Brahmavidya" (Jnana Yoga), "Yogashastr" (Karma Yoga), and "Shrikrishnarjunsamvad" (Bhakti Yoga) - all three. In the Gita, the dialogue of Shri Krishna and Arjuna begins and ends in devotion. At the beginning, Arjuna, being perplexed, seeks refuge in the Lord. "I am your disciple, teach me" (2.7) and at the end, the Lord's words "Come to me alone for refuge" (18.73) inspire Arjuna to take complete refuge. Arjuna had asked for a means to achieve his own well-being (2.7, 3.2, 5.1), so the Lord has also described "Jnana Yoga" and "Karma Yoga" in the Gita. First Chapter's Verses, Words, and Uvach

(1) In this chapter, there are three "Ath Prathamoadhyayah", twelve "Dhritarashtra Uvach", "Sanjaya Uvach" and so on, five hundred and eighty-four words, and thirteen words in the Gita's Pushpika. Thus, the total number of words is five hundred and eighty-four. (2) In this chapter, there are seven "Ath Prathamoadhyayah", thirty-seven "Dhritarashtra Uvach", "Sanjaya Uvach" and so on, one thousand five hundred and four words, and forty-eight words in the Pushpika. Thus, the total number of words is one thousand five hundred and fifty-two. (3) There are six "Uvach" in this chapter - one "Dhritarashtra Uvach", three "Sanjaya Uvach", and two "Arjuna Uvach". The meter used in the first chapter

In the forty-two verses of this chapter, the meter used in the fifth and thirty-third verses, and the third part of the forty-second verse is "Raganya" (R-vipula), and in the fifth verse and the third part of the ninth verse, it is "Naganya" (N-vipula). The remaining thirty-eight verses are in the "Pathyavaktra" meter, which is a characteristic of the Anushthup meter.

Arjuna had a conversation with Dronacharya and Duryodhana about the two armies, but Dronacharya did not say anything. This made Duryodhana unhappy. To please Duryodhana, Bhishma blew his conch loudly. After Bhishma's conch was blown, the conches of the Kauravas and Pandavas were also blown. Then, from the 20th verse, the dialogue between Shri Krishna and Arjuna began. Arjuna asked Lord Krishna to position his chariot in the middle of the two armies. Lord Krishna positioned the chariot in the middle of the two armies, in front of Bhishma and Drona, and asked Arjuna to look at the Kauravas. Seeing their own relatives in both armies, Arjuna was overcome with familial attachment, which led him to abandon the fight and sit in the middle of the chariot, with his bow and arrows. Lord Krishna then spoke to Arjuna, who was overcome with grief, as Sanjaya narrates to Dhritarashtra. Sanjaya said:
He, the one who is overcome with compassion and has eyes full of tears,
who is sorrowful and overcome with compassion,
spoke to him, the one who is overcome with compassion and has eyes full of tears,
the one who is sorrowful and overcome with compassion. Sanjaya said:
The one who is overcome with compassion, the one with eyes full of tears,
the one who is sorrowful and overcome with compassion,
spoke to him, the one who is overcome with compassion and has eyes full of tears,
the one who is sorrowful and overcome with compassion. Sanjaya

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 2

Thus spoke Madhusudana, the Lord of the Ganges, in this manner: "This divine word of mine is a direct blow." Arjuna, being overcome with cowardice due to the war, was comforted by the Lord, who then spoke the following words, which would be elaborated upon in the next two shlokas. Here, simply saying "" would have been sufficient, but saying " " is also necessary, as it implies that the Lord's words are extraordinary. This word, imbued with the essence of duty, has been donned by Arjuna, who has been overcome with the vice of renunciation. This word will awaken Arjuna's desire for his own well-being and will make him aware of his own defects. Due to the influence of this profound word, Arjuna will accept the Lord as his guru and take refuge in him (2.7). Sanjaya, by calling the Lord "," implies that the Lord is the one who destroys the wicked, like the demon Madhu. Therefore, the Lord will not rest until he has destroyed the wicked, like Duryodhana, and has brought them to an end. Relationship - What words did the Lord speak to Arjuna, and this will be explained in the next two shlokas. The Lord said:

Where have you come from, O Arjuna, and how has this weakness, which is unworthy of a noble person, and which does not lead to heaven, and which brings shame, come to be present in you, who are worthy of being served by noble people? Explanation - By saying "," the Lord is calling Arjuna, implying that he is a pure and untainted soul. Therefore, it is unnatural for cowardice to have arisen in him. The Lord's question "" implies that this weakness has not arisen from within Arjuna, but is an external influence that has taken hold of him. The Lord's words "" imply that this weakness has not only taken hold of Arjuna's thoughts and words, but also of his actions. It has taken hold of him so completely that he has abandoned his bow and arrow and taken his seat in the middle of the chariot. The Lord says, " " - "Where have you come from, O Arjuna, and how has this weakness, which is unworthy of a noble person, and which does not lead to heaven, and which brings shame, come to be present in you, who are worthy of being served by noble people?" The Lord is expressing his wonder at how such a weakness has arisen in Arjuna, who is a noble person, at a time when he should be showing bravery and enthusiasm for the war. There are two types of wonder: one that arises from not knowing something, and the other that arises from being awakened by someone else. The Lord's wonder is of the second type, and it is directed at Arjuna, in order to awaken him to his true nature. 1. Here, the word "" is used with the suffix "," which is a permanent suffix, as it is used in the Nitya Yoga. This is because the six qualities of the Lord - sovereignty, duty, fame, prosperity, knowledge, and detachment - are always present in him. 2. The compound "" is a negation of the compound "," which means that what is not desirable for noble people is what is desirable for non-noble people. If the negation were to be placed before the compound, it would mean that what is not desirable for noble people is what is desirable for non-noble people, which would not make sense.

Chapter 2, Verse 3

The verse 2.3 is the Sadhak-Sanjivani (the nectar of the seekers). 67
Therefore, in the latter part of the shloka, the Lord says that it is not even a means of gaining fame in this world. By saying the above words, He says that the cowardice that has arisen in you is not a means of gaining fame, but rather a means of gaining infamy. Therefore, a great person does not accept cowardice in you. The reason is that cowardice is entirely inappropriate. That is, there is no mention of your well-being in this cowardice. The seekers of well-being always keep their well-being in mind in both action and inaction. They do not generate cowardice towards their duties. According to the circumstances, they get the duty that comes to them, and they perform it with enthusiasm and eagerness, keeping the goal of achieving well-being in mind. They do not become inactive like you, who are cowardly, in the face of war or any other duty. Therefore, becoming inactive in the face of duty is not beneficial for you. 'Aswargyam' - If you do not keep your well-being in mind and look at it from a worldly perspective, then in the world, the heaven is considered superior. But your cowardice is not even a means of gaining heaven, i.e., the result of cowardly inaction is not even the attainment of heaven. The Lord has mentioned here 'Anaryajushtam', 'Aswargyam', and 'Akirtikaram' - in this order, three types of people. (1) Those who are thoughtful people, they only want their well-being. Their goal, objective is only to achieve well-being. (2) Those who are pious people, they want to attain heaven through good deeds. They consider heaven to be superior and keep its attainment as their goal. (3) Those who are ordinary people, they respect the world. Therefore, they want to gain fame in the world and consider it as their goal. By mentioning the above three, the Lord warns Arjuna that your decision not to fight is not even a means of achieving well-being, nor is it a means of attaining heaven, nor is it a means of gaining fame. 'Akirtikaram' - If, even without considering the attainment of heaven, your decision to not fight is due to attachment, then it is considered that a good person does only that which is considered lowly, which is a means of your downfall, which will take you to hell, and which will bring you infamy in the world. But your cowardice will be the cause of your downfall and your infamy. Relation - What to do after cowardice arises? To remove this curiosity, the Lord says:

Klabhyam ma sma gamah parth na etat tvayyupapadyate. Kshudram hridaya-daurbalyam tyaktvottishth parantap. Translation:

O Portha (son of Pritha), do not be a coward. It is not suitable for you. Leave aside this weakness of the heart and stand up, O Parantap (O Arjuna, the destroyer of enemies). Word-by-word breakdown:

- Hridaya-daurbalyam = weakness of the heart
- Klabhyam = cowardice
- Ma sma = do not be
- Gamah = inactive
- Parth = O Portha (son of Pritha)
- Na etat tvayyupapadyate = it is not suitable for you
- Tyaktvottishth = leave aside and stand up
- Parantap = O Parantap (O Arjuna, the destroyer of enemies)

Explanation - 'Parth' is a name given to Arjuna because he is the son of Pritha (Kunti). The Lord addresses Arjuna as 'Parth' to remind him that he is the son of his aunt (Pritha - Kunti) and also his dear friend and devotee. Therefore, the Lord tells him confidential things and says what is true and beneficial for him.

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 2

To arouse the spirit of bravery in Arjuna, Lord Krishna refers to him as 'Pārtha', which means freedom, heaven, or fame. This implies that he is not one who would succumb to cowardice. If you do not abandon this lowliness and do not disobey your mother's command, you will yourself become lowly; and (2) this weakness of the heart - 'Clābyaṃ mā sma gamaḥ' - is a weakness due to cowardice. You, like a brave warrior, consider waging war to be a sin and not waging war to be a virtue. Abandoning this weakness is not a difficult task. Therefore, to awaken Arjuna, Lord Krishna says that not waging war is not a matter of virtue, this is a sign of impotence (eunuchism). So, leave this impotence behind. 'Naivattvayyupapadyate' - This eunuchism should not have come to you; because you are the son of Kunti, a brave Kshatriya mother, and you yourself are a brave warrior. This implies that this eunuchism is entirely unsuitable for you from birth and from your nature. 'Tum parantapa' - You are yourself 'Parantapa', meaning one who burns and drives away enemies, so what will you do by fleeing from war and making your enemies happy? You think that I am a virtuous person and do not want to commit the sin of war, this is a weakness of your heart, a sign of your weakness. Leave this weakness behind and stand up for war, that is, fulfill your duty. Here, Arjuna's duty is to fight in the war. Therefore, Lord Krishna says, 'Get up, stand up and fulfill your duty of war'. Lord Krishna has no doubt in his mind about Arjuna's duty from all perspectives. He knows that for Arjuna, fighting is the only duty. Therefore, disregarding Arjuna's weak arguments, Lord Krishna gives him a stern command to fulfill his duty. Arjuna said:

'O Madhusudana, O Arisudana, I will fight with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, my friends.' 4

Explanation: 'Madhusudana' and 'Arisudana' - these two addresses mean one who kills the wicked and the enemies of the world, respectively. Kunti's message was:

'Tell Arjuna and Bhima, who are always eager for war, that the time has come for them to fulfill their duty, which is the reason why a Kshatriya mother gives birth to a son.' (Mahabharata, Udoyog 137.9-10)

Shloka 5:

* The Life-Saving Verse *
You have killed those who harbor hatred and cause harm, even enemies like them. However, in front of me, my grandfather Bhishma and teacher Drona are standing, who are extremely virtuous, have a great affection for me, and teach me lovingly. How can I kill such well-wishers of mine? 69

You have also killed the great demons, and those who have come with great love and affection towards me. Teacher Drona is revered by us due to his association with knowledge. He is my teacher. He has such affection for me that he has not taught his own son Ashwatthama as much as he has taught me. He has taught both of us how to use the Brahmastra, but he has only taught me how to conclude it, not his son. He has also given me a boon that "among my disciples, there will be no one greater than you in the arts of warfare and weapons." In this relationship, both my grandfather Bhishma and teacher Drona are revered and worthy of worship. They have the right to attack me, but how can I attack them with arrows? Fighting them as an adversary would be a grave sin for me, as they are worthy of service and worship. How can I kill such revered individuals? Relationship - The previous shloka had Arjuna excitedly telling Lord Krishna his decision. Now, due to the effect of Lord Krishna's words, Arjuna is balancing his own decision with that of Lord Krishna and says:

It would be better to kill the wise and noble gurus, even if it means eating alms in this world. However, to kill the gurus who are motivated by desire and worldly gain, and who are stained with blood, is to enjoy the pleasures of the world. 5

Note: The translation of the shloka is based on the Gita Press edition of the Bhagavad Gita. Commentary:

In this shloka, Arjuna is saying that it would be better to kill the wise and noble gurus, even if it means eating alms in this world. This shloka suggests that Arjuna is still hesitant to kill his gurus and is looking for a way out. The word "guru" in this shloka refers to the wise and noble individuals who are worthy of respect and worship. The word "arthakam" refers to the desire for worldly gain and pleasure. The word "ruthirapradigdhan" refers to the gurus who are stained with blood, implying that they are involved in violence and bloodshed. In this shloka, Arjuna is saying that it would be better to kill the gurus who are motivated by desire and worldly gain, rather than the wise and noble gurus. However, this is not a straightforward statement, and Arjuna is still struggling with his decision.

'Gurunahatva..... Bhikshyamapiha Lokhe' - Now Arjuna first says that before understanding his duty, he was standing in the Kauravas' favor. Presenting his own side, he says that if I do not fight with Bhishma, Drona, and other revered people, then Duryodhana will not fight with me alone. In this way, without a war, I will not get the kingdom, and I will suffer pain. My livelihood will also be difficult. To the extent that the profession of begging, which is forbidden for a Kshatriya, may have to be adopted for livelihood. But I consider it better to adopt the profession of begging, which is painful, than to kill the guru-janas. 'Tiha Lokhe' means that although begging and eating will bring shame and disrespect in this world, I consider it better than killing the guru-janas. ‘Api' means that both killing the guru-janas and begging are forbidden for me; but among these two, I consider killing the guru-janas to be more forbidden. 'Hatvarthakamanshtu Rudhirapradigdhan' - Now Arjuna, looking at the words of the Lord, says that if I fight according to your order, then in the war, I will have to kill the guru-janas whose blood will be stained, and who are motivated by the desire for wealth and other worldly pleasures. I will have to enjoy those pleasures. I will get those pleasures. There will be little freedom from them. There will be little peace. It can be asked here that if we consider 'Arthakamans' as the adjective of 'Gurun', then what is the objection? The answer is that it is not proper to consider 'Arthakamans' as 'Gurun' with the adjective 'Arthakamans'. Because Pitamaha Bhishma, Acharya Drona, etc. guru-janas were not motivated by the desire for wealth. They were the servants of Duryodhana, they ate Duryodhana's food. Therefore, at the time of war, leaving Duryodhana's side is... Another thing, Arjuna has used the word 'Mahanubhavans' for Bhishma, Drona, etc. Therefore, such great people cannot be called 'Arthakamans'. The meaning is that those who are great, they cannot be motivated by the desire for wealth, and those who are motivated by the desire for wealth, they cannot be great. Special note

The Lord had given Arjuna the order to fight in the second and third shlokas, looking at his welfare. But Arjuna has understood it in the opposite way, i.e., the Lord has given the order to fight for the sake of enjoying the kingdom. First, Arjuna had only one side of not fighting, due to which he had dropped his bow and arrow and sat in the middle of the chariot, overcome with grief (the 38th shloka of the first chapter). But the side of fighting was given by the Lord. The meaning is that Arjuna's thought was that we know the dharma, but Duryodhana and others do not know the dharma, therefore they are ready to fight for the sake of wealth, kingdom, etc. Now Arjuna is saying the same thing for himself that if I fight according to your order, then the result will be that I will get wealth, kingdom, etc. stained with the blood of guru-janas. In this way, Arjuna sees only evil in fighting. The evil that appears as evil is easy to remove. Arjuna said:

I see no end to my sorrow, even if I gain the kingdom of the earth (bhūmāu) and the sovereignty of the gods (surāṇām) in heaven (svar-gam). (7.74)

Explanation - Arjuna thinks that if he wins the war, he will get the kingdom of the earth, which will be prosperous and free from enemies, and he will be happy. But even if he gets such a kingdom, he will not be free from sorrow. He also thinks that even if he gets the sovereignty of the gods in heaven, he will not be free from sorrow. If I gain the kingdom of the earth, which is prosperous and free from enemies, and the sovereignty of the gods in heaven, I will still not be free from sorrow. (7.74)

Explanation - Arjuna says that even if he gets the kingdom of the earth, which is prosperous and free from enemies, and the sovereignty of the gods in heaven, he will still not be free from sorrow. He is not satisfied with material wealth and power. Even if I gain the kingdom of the gods in heaven, which is full of divine pleasures, I will still not be free from sorrow. (7.74)

Explanation - Arjuna says that even if he gets the kingdom of the gods in heaven, which is full of divine pleasures, he will still not be free from sorrow. He is not satisfied with divine pleasures. Sanjaya said:

Thus spoken to Hrishikesha, the son of Gudakesha, the annihilator of sleep, said nothing more. (9)

Explanation - Sanjaya says that after Arjuna spoke these words, he remained silent, having spoken his mind to Lord Krishna, the annihilator of sleep.

The dialogue of Shri Krishna and Arjuna begins and ends in devotion... In the Gita, the dialogue of Shri Krishna and Arjuna begins and ends in devotion, as it is said in the phrase " ". The meaning of "" is that God is the one who resides within the hearts of all beings, knowing their innermost thoughts and feelings. The phrase "" implies that God is speaking through Arjuna. Therefore, when Arjuna says "", it means that he is aware of God's presence within him. However, Arjuna's words seem to be filled with a sense of sorrow and attachment, which is actually a result of his attachment to worldly life and the fear of losing his family and kingdom. But in reality, Arjuna's words are not just a repetition of his sorrow, but also a sign of his inner turmoil and conflict. Perishable thoughts - The battlefield of Kurukshetra is divided into two parts, with the Kaurava army on one side and the Pandava army on the other. In the middle of the two armies, there is a magnificent chariot with white horses. On one side of the chariot is Lord Krishna, and on the other side is Arjuna. Lord Krishna begins to teach Arjuna the divine knowledge, starting with the description of the body and its parts. Relationship - To remove Arjuna's sorrow, Lord Krishna begins to explain the divine knowledge. The Supreme Lord said:
You are not lamenting over those who have not died,
nor those who have died. The wise do not grieve for the living or the dead. Translation of the shloka:

You are not lamenting over those who have not died (), nor those who have died (). The wise () do not grieve (, ) for the living () or the dead (). The reason for Arjuna's sorrow was that he had a biased attitude towards his family members and the Pandavas, considering them as his own and others as not his own. This biased attitude is a result of attachment and ego. The wise people do not grieve for the living or the dead, as they understand that everything is temporary and ephemeral. In the Gita, the first person to express sorrow is Dhritarashtra, who asks what his sons and the Pandavas did on the battlefield. Although the Pandavas are considered to be more worthy of respect than Dhritarashtra, he still has a sense of attachment towards his sons. Similarly, Arjuna also has a sense of attachment towards his family members and the Pandavas, but it is not the same as Dhritarashtra's attachment. Arjuna considers all the Kauravas as his own family members and says, " " (1.28), and also considers Duryodhana and others as his own family members, saying, " " (1.37). This means that Arjuna has a sense of attachment towards all the Kauravas, and it is this attachment that is causing him sorrow. To remove this sorrow, Lord Krishna teaches Arjuna the divine knowledge, which begins with this eleventh shloka.

english: Arjuna is overcome with grief, lamenting the loss of his relatives and friends who have been killed in the war. Shri Krishna tells Arjuna that the separation of the body and the soul is inevitable for all beings. Some have already experienced this separation, while others will experience it in the future. Therefore, there is no need to grieve. Shri Krishna says that if Arjuna grieves for the loss of his relatives, he will be taking their place in the cycle of birth and death. This will lead to the downfall of their family and the destruction of their lineage. Instead, Arjuna should focus on his own spiritual growth and development. Shri Krishna explains that the body is impermanent and ephemeral, while the soul is eternal and imperishable. The body is subject to decay and destruction, but the soul remains unchanged. Therefore, there is no need to grieve for the loss of the body. Arjuna is still overcome with grief, and Shri Krishna tells him that his grief is a sign of ignorance and lack of wisdom. Grief and lamentation are not a solution to the problem of death and destruction. Shri Krishna quotes two ancient texts to support his argument. The first text states that a person who laments the death of a loved one is like a person who is forced to eat the tears of the deceased. The second text states that the relatives of the deceased are the ones who shed tears on earth, while the deceased person drinks them in the afterlife. Shri Krishna tells Arjuna that he should not grieve for the loss of his relatives, but rather focus on their well-being and spiritual growth. He should not worry about their future or their ability to provide for themselves, but rather trust in the natural order of things. Shri Krishna concludes by saying that the root cause of all suffering and grief is the attachment to the body and the ego. As long as we identify ourselves with the body and the ego, we will experience suffering and grief. But if we can transcend this attachment and focus on our spiritual growth and development, we will find peace and liberation. The impermanence of the body is a fact of life, and it is not something to be grieved over. Arjuna's grief is a sign of ignorance and lack of wisdom. He is not able to see the bigger picture and understand the natural order of things. He is still attached to his ego and his body, and this attachment is causing him suffering and grief. Shri Krishna is trying to teach Arjuna a lesson. He is trying to show him that the key to happiness and liberation is not to grieve for the loss of the body, but rather to focus on spiritual growth and development. Arjuna needs to learn to let go of his attachment to the body and the ego, and instead focus on his spiritual growth and development. The dialogue between Shri Krishna and Arjuna is a classic example of the spiritual teachings of the Gita. Shri Krishna is trying to teach Arjuna the importance of detachment and the impermanence of the body. The Gita teaches us that the body is impermanent and ephemeral, while the soul is eternal and imperishable. The Gita also teaches us that grief and lamentation are not a solution to the problem of death and destruction. Instead, we should focus on our spiritual growth and development. We should learn to let go of our attachment to the body and the ego, and instead focus on our spiritual growth and development. The Gita is a spiritual text that teaches us the importance of detachment and the impermanence of the body. It teaches us that the key to happiness and liberation is not to grieve for the loss of the body, but rather to focus on spiritual growth and development.

भूतग्रामः स एवायम्' ( गीता ८ । १९), 'सर्गेऽपि नोपजायन्ते प्रलये न व्यथन्ति च' (गीता १४ । २ ) ।
-

Chapter 2, Verse 11-19

11. It is the duty to perform the rituals of offering food and water to the ancestors, and to make arrangements for the funeral rites of those who have passed away. It is the duty to make arrangements for the upkeep of those who are still alive. The consideration of duty is not a subject of worry, but rather a subject of thought. Through thought, one becomes aware of one's duty, and through worry, one's thought is destroyed. 12. The Lord has explained that the cause of Arjuna's worry is the fear of loss of those who have passed away and those who have not passed away. Those who have passed away are 'gatāsūn' (those who have gone), and those who have not passed away are 'agatāsūn' (those who have not gone). The Lord has also said, "The downfall of the ancestors occurs when the body and water do not reach them" (Gita 2.42). 13. Arjuna's worry about 'gatāsūn' is due to his attachment to the body, and his worry about 'agatāsūn' is not a worry at all. The worry about 'agatāsūn' is not a worry because even if one considers the distinction between good and evil, one should not worry about it. Similarly, even if one considers the distinction between good and evil, one should not worry about it. 14. The two worries, 'gatāsūn' and 'agatāsūn', are both transitory and ephemeral. The worry about 'gatāsūn' is due to the attachment to the body, which is ephemeral and transitory. The worry about 'agatāsūn' is due to the attachment to the body, which is ephemeral and transitory. 15. The Lord's teaching begins with the distinction between the body and the one who possesses the body. Other philosophical texts describe the distinction between the self and the non-self, but the Gita describes the distinction between the body and the one who possesses the body, as per the experience of all beings. 16. The Gita's teaching is unique in that it begins with the distinction between the body and the one who possesses the body. The sādhanā (spiritual practice) of the seeker of knowledge is to know himself, and the first step in this sādhanā is to know the distinction between the body and the one who possesses the body. 17. The body is ephemeral and transitory, and the one who possesses the body is eternal and immutable. The body is subject to constant change, while the one who possesses the body remains unchanged. The Gita says, "The universe is eternal, and it is not born or destroyed" (Gita 8.19). 18. The body and the one who possesses the body are both inscrutable. The body is constantly being destroyed, and therefore, it is not a subject of worry. The one who possesses the body is never destroyed, and therefore, it is not a subject of worry. 19. The worry about the body and the one who possesses the body is a sign of ignorance. The wise person knows that the body is ephemeral and transitory, and the one who possesses the body is eternal and immutable. The wise person knows that the body is subject to constant change, while the one who possesses the body remains unchanged.

. The self (atman) remains, but the body is constantly in a state of death. You do not suffer any loss, even a tiny bit, due to the body's damage. Therefore, you should not feel sorrow, anxiety, fear, and so on, while carrying the body. The body is not attached to any body, so it is said to be all-pervading - 'sarvagatah' (2.24), 'yena sarvam idam tatam' (2.17). The implication is that the self (atman) is only a state of existence; therefore, in reality, it is not a body (shariri) but is bodiless. That is why the Lord has also called it 'avikta' - 'avikta' (2.25), 'aviktaadinam bhutanam' (2.28). The body is constantly being destroyed and is unreal. There is no existence of the unreal - 'nasato vidyate bhava' (2.16). If there is no existence, how can the unreal body be considered a body (shariri)? Therefore, the self (atman) is neither a body nor a body (shariri). However, in this context, the Lord has called the self (atman) 'shariri' (dehi) for the sake of explaining it to the seekers. 'Shariri' means that you are not a body. When we think about the body and the body (shariri), they are the same at the time of thinking and at the time of not thinking. The state of the body and the body (shariri) does not change due to thinking or not thinking. The seeker's attachment is removed, and his human birth is successful. The human body is endowed with discrimination. Therefore, the realization 'I am not a body' can only be achieved in the human body. Considering the body as 'I' is not a human intellect but a beastly intellect. That is why Shri Shukadeva Maharaj says to King Parikshit:

"O King! Now, give up this beastly intellect that says 'I will die.' Just as the body was not born before, was born, and will die, similarly, you were not born before, were born, and will die - this is not true."

Relation - Why is it inappropriate to grieve for the self (atman) due to its existence - This question is answered in the next two shlokas. We were not present in the past, nor will we be present in the future. We were not present in the past, nor were you, nor were the kings. We will not be present in the future. This is the truth. Translation of Shloka 12.2:

We were not present in the past, nor were you, nor were the kings. Explanation - [Only two things exist in the world - the self (atman) and the body (shariri). Both are indestructible, i.e., they cannot be grieved for. The reason is that the self (atman) is eternal, and the body is constantly being destroyed. The word 'ashochyam' in the previous shloka is explained here as the eternity of the self (atman) and the impermanence of the body.]

It is not so. *
The Bhagavad Gita*
Here, saying "I, you, and these kings were not" would have been sufficient to make the point, but instead, it is said, "We were not, this is not the case." The reason for this is that saying "We were not, this is not the case" makes the point that "We were certainly there" becomes firmly established. The implication is that the eternal truth is always eternal. It never had a beginning, nor will it ever have an end. The phrase "jatu" means that in all three times - past, present, and future - and in all places, circumstances, states, events, and objects, there is no absence of the eternal truth, even in the slightest degree. Here, the Lord has used the word "aham" (I) to make a unique point. In the fifth verse of the fourth chapter, the Lord says to Arjuna, "I have had many births, and you have had many births, but I know them all, and you do not know them." In this way, the Lord has revealed His divine nature and distinguished Himself from the living beings. But here, the Lord is saying that He is one with the living beings. The implication is that in the former case, the Lord's intention was to reveal His greatness and special qualities, and in this case, His intention is to reveal the eternal truth. "It is not that we were not, and it will not be that we are not" - this is not the case. The Lord has said this about the past and the future, but not about the present. The reason for this is that in the present, we are all manifest, and there is no doubt about it. Therefore, there is no need to say, "We were not, and it will not be that we are not." If we look at the present from a philosophical perspective, we are all present, and the bodies are constantly changing. We should experience the separation from the bodies in the present itself. The implication is that just as there is no absence of our existence in the past and the future, so too there is no absence of our existence in the present. We should experience this. Just as every living being has the experience that "We are present" before falling asleep and after waking up, so too we were present in the same way when the bodies were not present, and we will be present in the same way when the bodies are not present. The only difference is that there was a lack of external knowledge, but our existence was not absent. Similarly, we are present in the same way now, and the bodies are constantly changing and moving towards destruction. But our existence is eternal, and it was present before, will be present after, and is present now. Our existence is a time-less truth, because we are aware of all three times - past, present, and future. The Lord has said this verse to explain this time-less truth. Special Point
It is not that we were not, and it will not be that we are not - this is not the case. The implication is that when the bodies were not present, we were present, and when the bodies will not be present, we will be present. The bodies are impermanent, and we are permanent. This proves the impermanence of the bodies and the permanence of our existence. The implication is that what is present at the beginning and end is also present in the middle, and what is not present at the beginning and end is also not present in the middle. If something is not present at the beginning and end, how can it not be present in the middle? The answer is that the way we perceive it is with the help of the mind, intellect, and senses, which are constantly changing. They are not stable for even a moment. When we identify ourselves with the perceived object and the perception, we become the perceiver. But when the perception and the perceived object are both changing, how can the perceiver be stable? The implication is that the name "perceiver" is given only in relation to the perception and the perceived object. If there is no relation between the perception and the perceived object, then there is no name for the perceiver, but the eternal truth that is the basis of the perceiver remains. [Chapter 2
Just as every living being has the experience that "We are present" before falling asleep and after waking up, so too we were present in the same way when the bodies were not present, and we will be present in the same way when the bodies are not present. We are aware of all three times - past, present, and future - because our existence is a time-less truth.
