and it is eternal and unchanging. Its truth is not affected by the existence or non-existence of the universe. One who has a vision of this truth cannot be affected by the thought of destruction or the darkness of ignorance. However, this foundation and illuminator can also be considered as dependent (adhey) or non-existent (anupalabdhi). In this context, I, you, and the kings are all unchangeable (ashochya) in our true nature (svarupa) as the seer and the illuminator. This verse describes the similarity between the Supreme Self (Paramatma) and the individual self (jiva-atma). The Lord says that we were not present in our present forms as Krishna, Arjuna, and kings in the past, nor will we be present in these forms in the future. However, in terms of our true nature (svarupa), we were present in the past, will be present in the future, and are present in the present. This means that we are all one in our true nature, but we are different in our physical bodies. Our bodies were not present in the past and will not be present in the future, but our true nature is eternal and unchanging. When our bodies were not present, our true nature was still present, and when our bodies are not present in the future, our true nature will still be present. There is only one eternal and unchanging reality (sattya-tattva). The phrase "I, you, and the kings" means that the true nature of the Supreme Self and the individual self is the same, i.e., "I am" (aham) and "I exist" (aham) are both expressions of the same eternal and conscious reality (chitmay sattya). "I am" (aham) is related to the seer (drashta), and if the seer is not present, then "I am" is not present. However, the reality of "I exist" (aham) remains, which is the true nature (svarupa) of the individual self. Therefore, we should not grieve over the change of bodies. The past, present, and future are all distant from us, just like the past and future are distant from us in the sense that we have no connection with them. Similarly, the present is also distant from us, and there is no connection between us and the present. Since there is no connection, what is the difference between the past, present, and future? These three periods of time are all within the scope of time, while our true nature is beyond time. Time is fragmented, but our true nature is unbroken. We consider the body as our true nature, which is why we see a difference between the past, present, and future. However, in reality, the past, present, and future do not exist. Even if many ages pass, the individual self (jiva) does not change, because it is a part of the Supreme Self (Paramatma). However, the physical body changes, and it remains for a moment only. In this body, as in the body of others, childhood (kumar), youth (yauvan), and old age (jara) come and go. Similarly, the attainment of another body (deha-antar-prapti) also comes and goes. A wise person is not disturbed by these changes. Translation of the shloka:

13. As in this body, the child, youth, and old age come and go, similarly, the attainment of another body comes and goes. A wise person is not disturbed by this.

The Bhagavad Gita

[ Chapter 2
If the body changes into another body, then there is also sorrow in this matter. The second point is that in the state of childhood and youth, when one sleeps, the body and senses feel refreshed, but in old age, when one sleeps, they do not feel refreshed, that is, in old age, one does not get the same rest as in childhood and youth. In this way, the change of the subtle body is proved. It should not be so. Just as, with the passage of time, a child, a youth, and so on, come to be in the gross body, similarly, with the passage of time, the subtle and causal bodies come to be in the state of transmigration, that is, just as the states of childhood, youth, and so on come to be in the gross body, similarly, the state of transmigration comes to be in the subtle and causal bodies. The change of states in the gross body is seen with the naked eye, but with subtle vision, it is seen that the change of states also takes place in the gross body. In childhood, the body was one way, in youth it was not that way, in fact, there is no moment when the change of the gross body does not take place. Similarly, in the subtle body, there is also a change of states, which is clearly seen in the form of transmigration. Now, we have to think about this: we have knowledge of the gross body, but we do not have knowledge of the subtle and causal bodies. Therefore, when we do not have knowledge of the subtle and causal bodies, how can we have knowledge of their change? The answer is that just as the knowledge of the gross body is based on its states, similarly, the knowledge of the subtle and causal bodies is also based on their states. The gross body is in the state of 'wakefulness', the subtle body is in the state of 'dream', and the causal body is in the state of 'deep sleep'. A man sees himself as a child in his childhood, as a youth in his youth, and as an old man in his old age. From this, it is proved that the subtle body also changes along with the gross body. In childhood, the state of deep sleep is more, in youth it is less, and in old age it is very little. Therefore, from this, it is also proved that the causal body changes. He who gets the body of a god, an animal, a bird, and so on, experiences 'I am this' in that body, due to the superimposition of the body. This is the change of the subtle body. Similarly, the causal body has a nature (principle) that is called habit in the gross vision. This habit is of a god, an animal, a bird, and so on. This is the change of the causal body. If there were a change in the body, then even with the change of states, the knowledge of 'I am the same' would not be there. But even with the change of states, the knowledge of 'I was a child, I was a youth, I am now the same' is there. From this, it is proved that there is no change in the self. A doubt may arise here: why does the knowledge of the previous body not remain even with the change of states? The reason is that there is great suffering at the time of death and birth. Due to this suffering, the memory of the previous birth does not remain. Just as, when one is struck by paralysis, or when one becomes very old, the knowledge of the previous state does not remain in the mind, similarly, at the time of death and birth, there is a great shock, due to which the knowledge of the previous birth does not remain. But he whose death is not accompanied by such suffering, that is, who gets the body of another person without any effort, his mind may remember the previous birth. Now, let us think about this: just as the knowledge of the change of states is there in the case of the change of bodies, similarly, the knowledge of the change of states is also there in the case of transmigration. 1 - In the case of transmigration, the gross body is left behind, but the subtle and causal bodies are not left behind until liberation takes place. As long as liberation does not take place, the subtle and causal bodies remain connected with the self. 2 - In the scriptures, this knowledge is called 'pratyabhijna' - 'tattvedan tava gahit jnanam pratyabhijna'. 3 - 'Manushya rote rute swanam uru vedenayastadhih' (Shrimad Bhagavat 3.30.18) - 'A man becomes unconscious due to great pain and dies in the midst of his weeping relatives.'

Vinishkranti krichchhren niruchchhwaso hatasmiti (Shrimad Bhagavat 3.31.23) - 'At the time of birth, his breathing stops and his previous memory is lost.'

4 - 'Ye mritya sahassa martya jayante sahassa punah. Tesam pauranik abhyasah kanchit kalam hi tisthati. Tasaj jatismarah lokhe jayante bodhasanyuta' (Mahabharat, Anushasan 145) - 'Those who are reborn, are reborn suddenly, and their previous knowledge remains for a short time. Those who are reborn with knowledge, are reborn with knowledge.'

Shloka 13]

* Sādha-kasāñjīvānī *

83
| The ignorant has gained knowledge. Such a steadfast person is never deluded by this subject, nor does he have any doubts. This does not mean that such a steadfast person attains transmigration of the soul. The cause of birth in high or low castes is the association of qualities, and when one is separated from qualities, a steadfast person can never attain transmigration of the soul. It is so, such knowledge does not occur in the attainment of transmigration; but 'I am' - such knowledge of one's own existence is always present in everyone. Just as, in deep sleep (suspension of consciousness), one has no knowledge of anything, but when one wakes up, one says, 'I had such a deep sleep that I had no knowledge,' then 'I had no knowledge' - this knowledge is present. Before falling asleep, I was what I am after waking up, so in the state of deep sleep also, I was the same - in this way, the knowledge of one's own existence remains unbroken and continuous. The knowledge of the absence of one's own existence is never present in anyone. The existence of the body remains unbroken and continuous, hence liberation occurs, and in the state of liberation, it remains so. However, in the state of liberation, one may not have knowledge of other bodies, but one experiences, 'I am separate from these three bodies' - such an experience does occur. The steadfast one does not get deluded - the steadfast one is he who has unbroken and continuous knowledge of the distinction between existence and non-existence. Here, the word 'tatra' does not mean 'in the subject of transmigration,' but rather 'in the subject of the body and the body's existence.' The meaning is that one should know what the body is, what the body's existence is, what is changeable, and what is unchangeable, what is impermanent, and what is permanent, what is non-existent, and what is existent, what is tainted, and what is untainted - in this subject, the steadfast one is never deluded. The body and the body's existence are entirely separate. He is never deluded in this subject - he has the understanding that the body is never one and the same, and the existence is never different. The body was not present before birth, will not be present after death, and is constantly dying in the present moment. In reality, the process of death and rebirth begins even in the womb. If the body dies in childhood, youth appears, if youth dies, old age appears, and if old age dies, transmigration to another body occurs. These are all states of the body. The three states of childhood, youth, and old age are states of the gross body, and transmigration to another body is a state of the subtle body and the causal body. However, the consciousness that is aware of the self is beyond all these states. The states change, but the self remains the same. In this way, the one who knows the distinction between the body and the self is never deluded in any state. The jiva (individual soul) experiences the fruits of its actions in various bodies, in hells and heavens - this is itself a proof that the 84 lakhs of bodies, hells, and heavens are left behind, but the jiva itself remains the same. The bodies change, but the jiva does not change. The jiva remains the same, and it is this that allows it to be born in various bodies, in various worlds. The one who is born in various bodies is not entangled with anything, is not bound anywhere. If it were entangled, then who would experience the 84 lakhs of bodies, who would go to hells and heavens, who would be liberated? Birth and death are not our dharma (righteous duty), but rather the dharma of the body. Our existence is beginningless and endless, within which various bodies are born and die. Just as we change various clothes, but the one who wears them does not change, similarly, in various bodies, our existence remains the same. The meaning is that our independence and distinction are self-evident. Our life is not bound to any one body. Because of our independence and distinction, we remain the same even in various bodies, but because of our association with the body, we take on various bodies. The association that is assumed to be true does not last, but we continue to take on new associations. If we do not take on new associations, then liberation (independence) and freedom are self-evident. The connection - the one who is connected to an impermanent thing, such as the body, experiences sorrow, and to get rid of this sorrow, one says, 'Those who suddenly attain death and then suddenly take birth again, their old habits or tendencies remain for some time. Therefore, they are born in the world with the knowledge of their past deeds and are known as jātismar. As they grow, their old memories, like a dream, gradually fade away.'

## Chapter 2
Oh Kounteya, the objects of the senses, such as touch, are indeed the sources of pleasure and pain, and are transient, coming and going. Oh Bharata, endure them. Commentary - Here, a doubt arises as to why these two verses (14 and 15) have been placed between the discussion of the self (atman) and the body (deha) in the preceding verses (11-13) and the subsequent verses (16-30). The solution to this is that just as in the 12th verse, the Lord explained His own eternal nature, saying "I was never not," and thus placed Himself in the same category as all other beings, so too here, in order to explain that the material body and other objects are impermanent and ephemeral, the Lord has discussed the topic of "mātrāsparśa" (objects of the senses). The word "tu" is used here to distinguish the eternal self (atman) from the impermanent objects of the senses. "Mātrāsparśa" refers to objects that can be perceived through the senses and the mind. The word "mātrā" means the means of measurement or perception, i.e., the senses and the mind. "Sparśa" means contact or connection. Therefore, "mātrāsparśa" refers to objects that can be perceived through the senses and the mind. As long as one does not reject the notion of a connection to these objects, that connection remains, even if the objects themselves are no longer present. For example, if a woman's husband has passed away, she is still referred to as his wife, even after many years. This shows that the connection remains, even if the object of that connection is no longer present. The words "śītoṣṇa" (cold and hot) here mean "anukūla" (favorable) and "pratikūla" (unfavorable). If we take them to mean only cold and hot, they would apply only to the sense of touch, which is limited to the skin. Therefore, it is more appropriate to interpret them as favorable and unfavorable. The objects of the senses, which are mere matter, give rise to pleasure and pain through their favorable and unfavorable nature. Here, the word "mātrāsparśa" refers only to objects, not to their connections. If we were to take "mātrāsparśa" to mean the connections between objects, we could not describe those connections as "āgamāpāyinaḥ" (coming and going), because the connection remains even after the objects themselves have gone. The connection is acknowledged only in the mind, and as long as that acknowledgment remains, the connection remains, even if the objects are no longer present. In reality, the objects themselves do not have the power to give rise to pleasure and pain. The pleasure and pain arise from the connection we make with them in our minds. This connection is not actually real, but rather a product of our imagination. It is only when we reject this imagined connection that it ceases to exist. No amount of physical renunciation, suffering, or change can eliminate this imagined connection; only the rejection of the notion of a connection can do so.

Shloka 14

Arjuna said:
O Krishna, the objects of the senses are seen as pleasant or unpleasant, and this perception of pleasantness or unpleasantness is present in every moment, just like fatigue. But in sleep, there is a sense of refreshment. Therefore, the Lord has said, "Sukhaduhkhadaah" (those that bring pleasure and pain), that the senses are constantly changing. The objects of the senses are "Aagamaapayinah" (those that come and go), that is, they are born and die, and they do not remain permanent. They were not present before their birth and will not be present after their death. Therefore, they are "Aagamaapayinah". If someone says that they remain in the middle, the Lord says that they do not remain even in the middle. They are constantly changing, and their change is so rapid that they cannot be seen in the same form again. Therefore, the Lord has said, "Anityaah" (those that are impermanent). Here, the Lord has described the objects of the senses as "Aagamaapayinah" in a gross sense and as "Anityaah" in a subtle sense. In the sixteenth shloka, He will describe them as "Asat" (those that do not exist) and the eternal truth as "Sat" (those that exist). The Lord says, "Tans-titikshasva" (bear them patiently), that is, do not consider the objects of the senses as pleasant or unpleasant. Do not let the perception of pleasantness or unpleasantness lead to attachment or aversion, joy or sorrow. Instead, remain detached and patient. The second aspect is that the body, senses, and mind are constantly changing, and their existence and non-existence are present. They are not a part of you, but you are the one who knows them. You remain the same, while they change. Therefore, remain detached and patient. Only the senses and the mind are impermanent and changing, while the objects of the senses are impermanent and changing. The knowledge of the objects of the senses is also impermanent and changing. The pleasure and pain that arise from the objects of the senses are also impermanent and changing. But the self remains the same, eternal, and unchanging. Therefore, bear them patiently. Do not consider the objects of the senses as pleasant or unpleasant. The objects of the senses are like cold and heat, which are both the same in the end. Similarly, pleasantness and unpleasantness are both the same. Therefore, the Lord says, "Titikshasva" (bear them patiently), that is, bear them patiently and remain detached. The pleasure and pain, joy and sorrow, attachment and aversion, and other changing emotions are all impermanent and changing. Therefore, bear them patiently and remain detached. It is a great mistake of the seeker to see the changing emotions and not see the self.

The Supreme Lord says:

That which is eternal and unchanging, yet appears to be changing, is not perceived by the senses, nor is it perceived by the mind, nor is it perceived by knowledge. It is not perceived by the one who perceives, nor by the one who is perceived. All these are within the realm of the changing circumstances (dasha). But the Supreme Self (Atman) is beyond all these changing circumstances. It is not perceived by the senses, nor by the mind, nor by knowledge. These perceiving and perceived ones are all within the realm of the changing circumstances. They will not remain, but the Supreme Self will remain. This is the meaning of the phrase "the perceiver is related to the perceived, and therefore the perceiver is called the seer (drashta)". If there is no relation with the perceived, then the Supreme Self will remain, but it will not be called the seer. Similarly, the Supreme Self is related to the body, and therefore it is called the embodied one (sari). If there is no relation with the body, then the Supreme Self will remain, but it will not be called the embodied one. Therefore, the Lord has called it the embodied one only for the sake of human beings. Relation - The previous shloka mentioned the importance of tolerating the touch of the material world. Now, the next shloka will explain what will happen as a result of this tolerance. Arjuna, the one who is the best among men, the one who is the embodiment of courage, the one who is the embodiment of wisdom, the one who is the embodiment of equanimity in the face of happiness and sorrow, the one who is the embodiment of the eternal and unchanging, is not perturbed by these changing circumstances (dasha). He is the one who has the power to attain immortality (amritatva). Explanation - The phrase "purusharshab" means that a man usually thinks of changing his circumstances, which cannot be changed and which cannot be altered. When Arjuna encountered the circumstances of war, he did not think of changing them, but instead thought of his own well-being. This is the mark of a great man. He is not perturbed by the changing circumstances. The phrase "samduhkhsukham dhira" means that a wise man is equanimous in the face of happiness and sorrow. The internal disposition of the mind is what makes a man happy or unhappy. The wise man is not affected by the external circumstances. He is the one who has the power to attain immortality. The phrase "yam hi na vyathayanti ete purusham" means that the wise man is not perturbed by these changing circumstances. The pleasure and pain that arise from the contact with the material world do not affect him. The pleasure that arises from the contact with the material world is not a cause of suffering, and the pain that arises from the contact with the material world is not a cause of suffering. The wise man is not affected by these changing circumstances. The phrase "so 'mritatvaaya kalpate" means that the wise man has the power to attain immortality. He has the power to attain immortality because he is not affected by the changing circumstances. He is not affected by the pleasure and pain that arise from the contact with the material world. He is the one who has the power to attain immortality because he has realized his true nature. The realization of his true nature is what gives him the power to attain immortality.

english: This human birth is not meant to enjoy happiness and sorrow, but to attain great bliss and supreme peace. After attaining this bliss and peace, there is nothing else to be achieved (Gita 6.22). If we are fortunate to have favorable circumstances, people, or situations, we will be happy, but this happiness will be accompanied by the desire to possess them, and we will not be able to utilize them properly. We will not have the power to utilize them properly because the power to utilize them will be spent in enjoying them, and we will not be able to utilize them; instead, we will only enjoy them. Similarly, if we are unfortunate to have unfavorable circumstances, people, or situations, we will be unhappy, and we will not be able to utilize them properly; instead, we will only suffer from them. We will not have the strength to bear the suffering because our strength will be spent in suffering, and we will not be able to bear it; instead, we will only suffer. If we use the favorable circumstances, people, or situations for our own happiness and comfort, and become satisfied with them, then this is the enjoyment of favorable circumstances. But if we use them for the service of the unfortunate, then this is the proper utilization of favorable circumstances. Therefore, we should consider the favorable circumstances as the property of the unfortunate. Now, let us consider how to utilize the unfavorable circumstances properly. The cause of suffering is the desire for happiness and the hope for it. Unfavorable circumstances become suffering-producing only when there is a desire for happiness within. If we give up the desire for happiness and the hope for it, then unfavorable circumstances will not be able to cause us suffering; instead, we will be happy with them. Just as a patient takes bitter medicine to get rid of the disease, and although it causes pain, he is happy because he knows that the disease will be cured. Similarly, if we take the bitter pill of suffering, which is the unfavorable circumstances, and give up the desire for happiness and the hope for it, then we will be happy with it. This is the proper utilization of unfavorable circumstances. If we continue to enjoy happiness and suffering, then in the future, we will have to go to the realms of birth and death, such as heaven and hell. This is because these realms are the places where happiness and suffering are enjoyed. If we do not rise above happiness and suffering, then how can we be eligible for liberation? We are only interested in enjoying happiness and suffering, so how can we be eligible for liberation? As mentioned in the 14th shloka, the Lord said that these worldly objects and circumstances are the causes of happiness and suffering, and they come and go, but they are not permanent; they are ephemeral and transitory. They are not always present, and they do not always remain. As soon as they are obtained, they begin to be destroyed, and as soon as they are obtained, they begin to be separated. They were not present before, and they will not be present after; they are constantly disappearing in the present moment. We are only enjoying them, and by enjoying them, we are only spoiling our nature, making ourselves into happiness- and suffering-enjoyers. By enjoying happiness and suffering, we are only making ourselves eligible for birth and death, and how can we be eligible for liberation?

How will God grant us liberation? In the Gita, the dialogue of Shri Krishna and Arjuna begins and ends in devotion... If we use the body for its intended purpose, we will rise above pleasure and pain. In this way, if we do not enjoy pleasure and pain and experience great joy, then our true nature, which is blissful, will be revealed. The true nature is beyond duality; it is beyond all forms of existence. The body is a form of existence, and when we identify with it, we experience pain. Therefore, no one can be free from pain as long as they identify with the body. To be free from pain means to be happy when we meet with what we love and not to be unhappy when we meet with what we do not love. This is the meaning of being free from pain (Gita 5.20). When we are free from pain, our mind becomes stable - 'sthirabuddhirsammoohah' (Gita 5.20). Being happy or unhappy is what we experience due to the presence of pleasure and pain. Enjoying pleasure and pain is what we experience. The person who enjoys pleasure and pain can never be happy. The seeker should not enjoy pleasure and pain but should use them for their intended purpose. Using pleasure and pain for their intended purpose is the true goal of human life. This goal is the attainment of immortality. Using pleasure for its intended purpose means serving others and bringing them joy. Using pain for its intended purpose means giving up the desire for pleasure. When we use pain for its intended purpose, we seek the cause of pain. The cause of pain is the desire for pleasure - 'ye hi samsparshaja bhoga duhkhayon eva te' (Gita 5.22). The person who enjoys pleasure and pain is ruined, and the person who uses pleasure and pain for their intended purpose is elevated above both pleasure and pain and experiences immortality. Relation - The discussion of the body and the self that has taken place so far is explained by God in the next three shlokas in different words. There is no existence of the non-existent, and there is no non-existence of the existent. Both have been seen by the seers of truth. 16. The non-existent has no existence, and the existent has no non-existence. Explanation - Here (in the first half of the shloka), God has used the three verbs 'bhav', 'abhav', and 'vidyate' to convey the idea of the eternal nature of the self. The three verbs are used to convey the idea that the self is eternal and unchanging. The non-existent has no existence - The body did not exist before its birth, and it will not exist after its death. In the present moment, it is constantly changing and does not exist in a permanent form. Therefore, the body is non-existent. The existent has no non-existence - The self existed before the birth of the body, and it will exist after the death of the body. In the present moment, the self is not affected by the changing body and remains the same. Therefore, the self is existent. In the same way, the world also has no existence. It is non-existent. The body is a small part of the world, and its changes are experienced as the changes in the world. Therefore, the world also has no existence. Seen - Experienced, realized. The world is constantly being consumed by the fire of time, just like a log of wood. When a log of wood is consumed by fire, it leaves behind ash and coal, but the world is consumed by time in such a way that nothing remains. Therefore, it is said that the non-existent has no existence.

english: and it is a dialogue of the eternal soul (Atman) and the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman). We can only see the world once, not twice, because the world is constantly changing. Just as a movie screen appears to be stationary, but in reality, the images on it change rapidly due to the speed of the film, so too does the world change rapidly, but we cannot perceive this change because of its speed. Moreover, the world is not even perceived as it truly is. This is because the means by which we perceive the world - the body, senses, mind, and intellect - are themselves part of the world. Therefore, it is the world itself that appears to us as the world. That which is beyond the world, and is unrelated to it, is not perceived at all. This means that the world is not perceived in its true nature. The perception of the world arises only from its relationship with the world. From this, it is clear that the true nature of the world is unrelated to the world itself. The second point is that the conscious essence (chit) cannot function without the assistance of the world (body, senses, mind, and intellect). This means that action and its consequences (Karma) occur only in the world, not in the true nature of the world. Since the true nature of the world is unrelated to action and its consequences, it is clear that the entire world, including the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is non-existent. The true nature of the world is action and its consequences, and matter. Since the true nature of the world is unrelated to both action and matter, it is clear that the entire world is non-existent. Only the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman) exists, which is the source of light and the foundation of all. Great souls have understood this truth and have distilled it to its essence, which is that only one eternal truth (Sat) exists. The essence of both the eternal truth (Sat) and the non-eternal (Asat) is also the eternal truth (Sat). Therefore, the eternal truth (Sat) is the essence of both. This eternal truth (Sat) is the one that is known by great souls who have understood the true nature of both the eternal truth (Sat) and the non-eternal (Asat). The power that appears to be non-eternal (Asat) is actually the power of the eternal truth (Sat). The non-eternal (Asat) appears to be powerful because of the power of the eternal truth (Sat). This eternal truth (Sat) is also known as the "higher nature" (Gita 7.5), the "knower of the field" (Gita 13.1-2), the "person" (Gita 13.19), and the "imperishable" (Gita 15.16). On the other hand, the non-eternal (Asat) is known as the "lower nature", the "field", the "nature", and the "perishable". Arjuna is grieving because he thinks that the bodies of his friends and relatives will perish if they fight in the war. But Lord Krishna says that even if they do not fight in the war, their bodies will still perish. The non-eternal (Asat) will perish, and it is constantly perishing. However, the eternal truth (Sat) that is present in them will never perish. Therefore, Arjuna's grief is due to his lack of understanding. In the eleventh shloka, it is said that wise people do not grieve for those who have died or are still alive. In the twelfth to thirteenth shlokas, it is said that the body is eternal, and in the fourteenth to fifteenth shlokas, it is said that the world is non-eternal. In all these shlokas, the word "dhira" (wise) is used. In this shloka, the word "tattvadarshi" (one who has understood the true nature) is used. The meaning of these words is that those who are wise and understanding do not grieve. If someone grieves, it means that they have not understood the true nature of both the eternal truth (Sat) and the non-eternal (Asat). The phrase "ubhayorapi drishto'ntastvayos tatvadarshibhih" means that those who have understood the true nature of both the eternal truth (Sat) and the non-eternal (Asat) do not grieve. Appendix: The eternal truth (Sat) alone is eternal, and everything else in the world, including the world itself, is non-eternal (Asat). Those great souls who have seen the true nature of both the eternal truth (Sat) and the non-eternal (Asat) have understood that the eternal truth (Sat) alone exists. Their vision (understanding) is that the power of the non-eternal (Asat) is also the power of the eternal truth (Sat). The phrase "yad yad vibhati bhootani bhavanti n bhavanti cha" means that although the bodies of living beings are constantly being born and dying, their birth and death are not visible due to the rapid movement of time. The phrase "na anushochanti panditah" means that wise people do not grieve. The phrase "dhira tatrah na muhhyati" means that the wise do not grieve. The phrase "samduhkh-sukham dhira" means that the wise are equal in happiness and sorrow. These three phrases are used to describe those who are wise and understanding.

Here, it is said that there is neither existence nor non-existence of the universe, i.e., the universe exists only as a manifestation of the Supreme Consciousness (Brahman). In the 14th and 15th shlokas, the Lord described the impermanence of the body, which is mentioned here as 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ' (the existence of non-being is not seen). In the 12th and 13th shlokas, the Lord described the permanence of the body, which is mentioned here as 'nābhāvo vidyate satḥ' (the non-existence of being is not seen). The phrase 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ nābhāvo vidyate satḥ' (the existence of non-being is not seen, and the non-existence of being is not seen) contains the essence of all the Vedas, Puranas, and Shastras. This phrase is used to describe the two fundamental principles of the universe, namely, the perishable (asat) and the imperishable (sat), which are also referred to as the material and spiritual worlds, the temporary and eternal, the destructible and indestructible, and so on. Whatever appears in the process of seeing, hearing, understanding, thinking, and deciding is all 'asat' (non-being). The instrument by which we see, hear, think, and decide is also 'asat'. The object that is seen is also 'asat'. In this sixteen-syllable phrase, three verbs are used:

(1) 'bhū' (to be) - as in 'abhāvaḥ' (non-existence) and 'bhāvaḥ' (existence). (2) 'as' (to be) - as in 'asat' (non-being) and 'sat' (being). (3) 'vid' (to be) - as in 'vidyate' (exists) and 'na vidyate' (does not exist). Although these three verbs have the same root meaning of 'existence', they have subtle differences in their meanings. The verb 'bhū' means 'origin' or 'birth', 'as' means 'existence' or 'being', and 'vid' means 'presence' or 'existence'. The phrase 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ' means that the existence of non-being is not seen, i.e., the non-being does not exist. The reason is that non-being is constantly changing and has no permanent existence. Non-being is not present, non-being is not obtained, non-being is not acquired, non-being is not available, non-being is not permanent. Whatever is produced will eventually perish, and this is a universal law. The destruction of a thing is so rapid that it cannot be seen twice in the same state. The principle is that if a thing has no existence at any moment, it has no existence at all. Therefore, the universe has no existence at all. No matter how much existence is attributed to it, no matter how much importance is given to it, in reality, it does not exist. Non-being is not obtained, non-being has never been obtained, non-being will never be obtained. It is impossible for non-being to be obtained. The phrase 'nābhāvo vidyate satḥ' means that the non-existence of being is not seen, i.e., the being exists. The reason is that being is constantly present and has no change. Being is always present, being is always existing, being is always available, being is always permanent. There is no moment, no place, no thing, no person, no action, no event, no situation, etc., in which the existence of being is not seen. Being is always the same, without any change or variation. The wise men who have seen the truth have not created the being, but have seen it, i.e., they have experienced it. They see only one being, which is the ultimate reality. They see that both non-being and being are one being, and that this being is the ultimate reality. They see that there is no separate existence of non-being and being, but only one being.

Shloka 17:
The absence of the unmanifest (asat) is proven by its non-existence, and the absence of the manifest (sat) is proven by its non-existence. Thus, it is established that the unmanifest does not exist, and the manifest alone exists. In the manifest, there is no distinction between the body and the self (atman). As long as the unmanifest exists, there is discernment (vivek). When the unmanifest is eliminated, discernment transforms into knowledge of the ultimate reality (tattvajnan). The wise ones who have realized the ultimate truth have seen both the unmanifest and the manifest within themselves. In this, "vivek" is discernment, "antah" is knowledge of the ultimate reality, and "drishtah" is the experience. Thus, discernment has transformed into knowledge of the ultimate reality, and only the existence of the ultimate reality remains. The existence of the unmanifest is not true, and the absence of the manifest is also not true. This is the ultimate truth of the path of knowledge. The seeker must accept the existence of the ultimate reality, whether or not they have experienced it. To accept "is" and reject "is not" is the essence of Vedanta, the ultimate conclusion of the Vedas. In the world, both existence and non-existence appear to exist, but non-existence is the primary reality. In the ultimate reality, both existence and non-existence appear to exist, but existence is the primary reality. In the world, non-existence encompasses both existence and non-existence, and in the ultimate reality, existence encompasses both existence and non-existence. In other words, in the world, there is "nitya-vyoga" (eternal separation) encompassing both union and separation, and in the ultimate reality, there is "nitya-yoga" (eternal union) encompassing both union and separation. Relationship: The nature of sat and asat will be explained in the next two shlokas. Avinashi tu tadvidhi yena sarvam idam tatam. Vinasam avyayasya asya na kascit kartum arhati. Avinashi, avinashi (the imperishable, the imperishable)

17. Translation:
Know that imperishable reality by which all this is pervaded. No one can cause destruction to the imperishable reality. Explanation: "Avinashi tu tadvidhi" - This is a continuation of the previous shloka, where it was said that "is not" is not true. Here, the nature of "is" is being explained. The word "tu" indicates that the explanation of "is" is being given. The word "tad" refers to the ultimate reality, which is being described as imperishable. The word "vidhi" means to know or understand. The phrase "yena sarvam idam tatam" means that the ultimate reality is pervading all this. The word "vinasam" means destruction, and "avyayasya" means imperishable. The phrase "asya na kascit kartum arhati" means that no one can cause destruction to the imperishable reality.

The Lord said:

In the case of weapons made of iron, iron is the essence, and in the case of vessels made of clay, clay is the essence. Similarly, in the case of snow made of water, water is the essence. In the same way, in the world, that eternal essence is present in all things. Therefore, it is indeed worthy of being known in this world. The body is imperishable (avyaya), for it is said, "No one can cause destruction to that which is indestructible" (vinashamavyasyasya na kashcit kartum arhati). However, the body is perishable, for it is constantly moving towards destruction. Therefore, the destroyer of the perishable body cannot be stopped. But, in reality, there is no difference in the outcome whether you engage in battle or not. The imperishable essence will remain, and the perishable body will perish. Here, the word "asya" (of this) refers to the eternal essence, implying that the essence that appears to be changing in every moment is indeed this eternal essence. The Lord has used this word "asya" to convey the idea that the essence that is present in every moment is the same eternal essence. The phrase "my body is this, and I am the one who dwells in this body" is the essence of self-awareness, and the Lord has used this phrase to convey the idea that the essence that is present in every moment is the same eternal essence. In our daily experience, we say, "This is a man, this is an animal, this is a tree, this is a house," and so on. However, the essence that is present in all these things is the same eternal essence. The things that we perceive as different are indeed different, but the essence that is present in all of them is the same. Similarly, I am a man, I am an animal, I am a god, and so on, but the essence that is present in all of these is the same. The phrase "yena sarvam idam tatam" (by which all this is pervaded) is used here to refer to the jiva-atma (individual self), and in the 21st verse of the 8th chapter and the 42nd verse of the 18th chapter, it is used to refer to the paramatma (supreme self). The meaning of this phrase is that the jiva-atma is pervaded by the paramatma, just as the paramatma is pervaded by the universe. Therefore, just as the paramatma is not affected by the universe, the jiva-atma is also not affected by the body and the world. The jiva-atma is not bound to any particular body or world; it is free and unattached. However, due to a lack of awareness of this fact, the jiva-atma is subject to birth and death. The imperishable (anashinah) and the unperceivable (aprameyas) essence is not affected by any change or destruction. It is not bound by any law or principle. The body, on the other hand, is perishable (antavantah) and is subject to destruction. Therefore, Arjuna, you should fight (yudhyasva). Explanation: The word "anashinah" refers to something that is not subject to destruction or change. It is something that is imperishable and indestructible. The word "aprameyas" refers to something that is not perceivable or knowable through the senses or the mind. It is something that is beyond the reach of the senses and the mind. The word "sharinah" refers to the body, which is subject to destruction and change. The phrase "uktah dehah" refers to the body, which is subject to destruction and change. The word "tasmad" means "therefore" or "hence." The phrase "yudhyasva" means "you should fight." The word "bharta" means "Arjuna."

The Lord has used the word "avyaya" to refer to both the body and himself. Although both are avyaya (imperishable) by nature, the Lord is free and unattached, while the body is bound by the laws of nature and is subject to destruction. The Lord is free to come and go as he pleases, while the body is bound to the cycle of birth and death.

* Sādhanasājīvanī *

This is a subject of faith, not of proof. The scriptures and the saints do not compel anyone to have faith in them. Man is free to have faith or not to have faith. If he has faith in the words of the scriptures and the saints, then this truth is his subject of faith; and if he does not have faith, then this truth is not his subject of faith. 'Nityasya' - This is the eternal and unchanging one. It does not cease to exist at any time. That is, it exists in all times. 'Antavant ime dehā uktaḥ śarīrīṇaḥ' - All the bodies in this world, which are imperishable, incomprehensible, and eternal, are said to be transient. The meaning of 'transient' is that their end is constantly approaching. There is nothing else in them except their end - only end - only end. In the above verses, the word 'dehā' (body) is used in the singular form, and 'śarīrīṇaḥ' (bodies) is used in the plural form. The reason for this is that each living being has three bodies - the gross, the subtle, and the causal. The other reason is that the same body-consciousness pervades all the bodies in the world. In the 24th shloka, it will be said that this body-consciousness is 'sarvagataḥ' (all-pervading). This body-consciousness is eternal, and the bodies that are said to be transient are perishable. Just as the eternal one cannot be destroyed, similarly, the perishable one cannot be made eternal. The perishable one will always remain perishable. Special Note

Here, 'antavant ime dehā' means that all the bodies that are seen are transient. But what are these bodies? 'Nityasya', 'anāśinaḥ' - these bodies are eternal, imperishable. The meaning is that the eternal truth has taken these bodies as its own, and these bodies have taken the eternal truth as their own. This means that the eternal truth has taken its abode in these bodies, and these bodies have taken their abode in the eternal truth. When the eternal truth takes its abode in these bodies, 'ahanta' (I am) arises, and when these bodies take their abode in the eternal truth, 'mamatā' (mine) arises. When one takes one's abode in these things, 'I am' arises in them; just as - when one takes one's abode in wealth, 'I am wealthy'; when one takes one's abode in the kingdom, 'I am the king'; when one takes one's abode in knowledge, 'I am learned'; when one takes one's abode in wisdom, 'I am wise'; when one takes one's abode in spiritual powers, 'I am accomplished'; when one takes one's abode in the body, 'I am the body'; and so on. When one takes one's abode in these things, 'mine' arises in them; just as - when one takes one's abode in the family, 'the family is mine'; when one takes one's abode in wealth, 'wealth is mine'; when one takes one's abode in wisdom, 'wisdom is mine'; when one takes one's abode in the body, 'the body is mine'; and so on. The arising of 'I am' and 'mine' with the jadedness is the only cause of vices. The meaning is that the body and the self are different, and if one does not give importance to this discrimination, vices arise. But those who give importance to this discrimination are wise. They never grieve, because they have the correct understanding that the truth is truth and the untruth is untruth. 'Tasmāt yudhyasva' - The Lord gives the order to Arjuna to fight, understanding the truth of the eternal and the transient. That is, the body is transient, and the body-consciousness is eternal. From this point of view, grief cannot arise. Therefore, give up grief and fight. In these 17th and 18th shlokas, the special feature is the discussion of the truth of the eternal. The reason is that the Lord's goal in this entire chapter is to make Arjuna understand the truth of the eternal. When the truth of the eternal is understood, the untruth is automatically eliminated. 1. In the beginning, this truth is a subject of faith, but when its direct experience is obtained, it is no longer a subject of faith. 2. Here, the word 'tasmāt' is used in the sense of 'yukti' (reasoning). That is, when the reasoning is understood, then fight. In the Gita, the word 'tasmāt' is used frequently at the end of a chapter or at the end of a reasoning. For example, in the 2nd chapter, 30th shloka, 3rd chapter, 19th shloka, 8th chapter, 7th shloka, and 27th shloka, and so on.

english:
Chapter 2, Verse 19

The one who knows this (the imperishable self) as the slayer and the one who considers it as slain, both of them do not know it. This (self) does not slay, nor is it slain. (atman)

Commentary:
The one who considers the self (atman) as the slayer (hantram) and the one who considers it as slain (hata) are both mistaken. This self (atman) does not slay, nor is it slain. (atman)

Explanation:
Just as a craftsman considers the body as the one to be killed, but does not truly understand it, similarly, the one who considers the self (atman) as the slayer and the one who considers it as slain are both mistaken. The self (atman) is imperishable and does not undergo any change. It is not subject to birth or death.

english:
Shloka 20:
The two - the one who thinks this body can be killed and the one who thinks it is killed - do not know. The one who thinks this body can be killed is also not correct, and the one who thinks it is killed is also not correct. This body cannot perform any action, just like it cannot exist without a body. It cannot do anything on its own. Therefore, in the 13th chapter, the Lord has said that all kinds of actions are done through the agency of nature - this is the experience of one who experiences the body as non-doer (tretiya adhyay ka untiya shloka). The meaning is that there is no doer in the body, but by identifying with the body and associating with it, one considers oneself the doer of actions that occur through the body. If one does not associate with the body, then one is not the doer of any action. The question arises: Does the one who thinks this body can be killed and is killed know correctly? The answer is that he also does not know correctly. The reason is that this body is not actually like that. It is not a killer and is not killed. It is eternal and unchanging, existing in its own nature. Therefore, one should not grieve for this body. The one who thinks this body is killed is also not correct. Just as this body is not a killer, so it is not killed; because in it, there is no change or transformation. Whatever is subject to change and transformation is born and dies. This body is free from all kinds of actions and is not a doer. In the presence of Arjuna, the context of war has arisen, so this body is described as being free from the actions of killing and being killed. In reality, this body is not a doer of any action, nor is it a doer of any karma, and in it, there is no change or transformation. The one who considers the body to be a killer and killed is actually not aware of the body's nature and does not understand its distinction from the body. The question arises: Why is this body not killed? The answer is that it is not born, it does not die, it does not change, it does not increase, it does not decrease, and it does not perish. It is eternal, unchanging, and immortal. The Lord says:




This body is not born, it does not die, it does not change, it does not increase, it does not decrease, and it does not perish. It is not killed even when the body is killed. The explanation is that there are six changes that occur in the body - birth, growth, increase, decrease, transformation, and death. This body is free from all these changes. The Lord is saying that this body is not born, it does not die, it does not change, it does not increase, it does not decrease, and it does not perish. The six changes are:

1. - It is born. 2. - It changes. 3. - It increases. 4. - It decreases. 5. - It perishes. The Lord is saying that this body is not subject to any of these changes.

96

The Bhagavad Gita

Chapter 2

This is not something that comes into existence; it has always been so. The Lord has said that as the body ages, its strength decreases, the senses weaken, and the body begins to decay. In this way, the body, senses, and mind undergo a process of decay, but the body itself does not decay. There is no decrease in this eternal reality. It is called "sanatana" (eternal) because it is said, "I am the eternal seed of all living beings, and I am the source of all life" (15.7). This body never dies. Only that which is born dies, and the term "mriyate" (dies) is used only when there is a separation of the body and the life force. The separation of the body and the life force occurs in the body, but the body itself does not undergo both union and separation. It remains as it is. The two main vikaras (disturbances) are birth and death. Therefore, the Lord has prohibited these two vikaras twice: first, "na jayate" (does not come into existence), and then again, "ajah" (does not come into existence); and first, "na mriyate" (does not die), and then again, "na hanyate hanyamane shareere" (does not die even when the body dies). "This is eternal, and it will not be born again" - this eternal reality is not born and will not be born again. It is self-existent and unchanging. Just as a child is born and then exists, but before birth, there is no existence, so this reality exists eternally and is not born. "ajah" - this body is never born. Therefore, it is called "ajah" (unborn). "This is eternal" - this reality is always the same, unchanging, and eternal. It does not undergo any transformation or change. It is always the same. "purana" - this reality is eternal and ancient, having no beginning. It is so old that it has never been born. Just as objects that are born and grow old eventually decay and do not grow again, this reality is not born and therefore cannot decay. "na hanyate hanyamane shareere" - even when the body dies, this eternal reality does not die. Here, the word "shareere" (body) is used to indicate that the body is destroyed. In the body, there are six vikaras (disturbances), but not in the reality itself. The Lord has given a clear description of the body and the reality in these verses, which is not found anywhere else in the Gita. Arjuna was particularly distressed by the prospect of his family members dying in the war. To alleviate his distress, the Lord says that even when the body dies, this reality does not die, and therefore, there is no reason to grieve. "This is eternal" - this reality is eternal and always exists. Therefore, it never undergoes decay. Decay occurs only in things that are not eternal. "Just as the parichita (distinct) nature of the self and the body is different, so too is the nature of the self and the body different. The self is not attached to the body, and the body is not attached to the self. Therefore, when the body dies, the self is not affected. We have discarded countless bodies in the past, but our existence has not been affected. We remain as we are - 'bhutagranah sa evaayam bhutva bhutva praliyate' (Gita 8.19). Similarly, when this body is shed, we will remain as we are. "Just as the hands, feet, and nose are parts of the body, so too is the body a part of the self. However, that which is born and undergoes change is not a part. Just as kapha (phlegm), mutra (urine), and other bodily fluids are born and undergo change, and just as a boil or other bodily afflictions are born and undergo change, so too is the body born and undergoes change. Therefore, the body is not a part of the self."

21. The imperishable (avvyayam) and eternal (nityam) person, who is devoid of birth (ajam) and is known by the Vedas (veda-avinashinam), how can he kill (ghatayati) or be killed (hanati) this body (enam)? Commentary:
Hail, Pritanandana! The person who has realized that the body is imperishable (avvyayam), eternal (nityam), birthless (ajam), and devoid of any change (avinashinam), how can he kill or be killed? The person who has realized this truth cannot be a killer or be killed. He cannot be the doer (kartaa) or the object of action (karma-yita). 22. Just as a man gives up old clothes and takes new ones, similarly, the embodied soul (dehi) gives up old bodies and takes new ones. Commentary:
Just as a man gives up old clothes and takes new ones, similarly, the embodied soul (dehi) gives up old bodies and takes new ones. This is the nature of the soul, which is eternal and imperishable. It is not bound by the cycle of birth and death, and it does not undergo any change. The soul is like a traveler who changes his clothes and vehicles, but remains the same.

as it is said in the previous chapter, the thirteenth shloka, that the person with a steady mind does not grieve about the change of bodies. Now, they are explaining this with an example, that just as a person does not grieve about changing old clothes, similarly, one should not grieve about changing bodies. Clothes are changed by humans, not by animals or birds; therefore, in this example of changing clothes, the word '' (man) is used. This word '' refers to human birth and includes both men and women, children and adults, young and old. Just as a person leaves old clothes and takes on new ones, similarly, the dweller of the body (dehi) leaves old bodies and takes on new ones. The old body is left behind and is called 'death', and the new body is taken on and is called 'birth'. As long as there is a relationship with nature, the dweller of the body keeps leaving old bodies and taking on new ones, according to one's actions and the thoughts at the time of death. Here, the use of the plural '' (bodies) implies that as long as the body does not realize its true nature, it continues to take on new bodies in an endless cycle. It is impossible to count how many bodies it has taken on so far. This idea is kept in mind while using the plural '', and the word '' (dweller of the body) is used to refer to all living beings. In the first half of the shloka, the old clothes are mentioned, and in the second half, the old bodies are mentioned. How can the example of old clothes be applied to old bodies? The reason is that bodies die not only at old age but also in childhood and youth. Therefore, the example of old clothes cannot be applied to old bodies. The answer is that bodies die only when their life span is over, and this is what is meant by '' (old). Whether it is a child's body, a young person's body, or an old person's body, they all become old when their life span is over. *

Chapter 2

In this shloka, the Lord has used the words '' (like) and '' (thus) to say that just as a person leaves old clothes and takes on new ones, similarly, the dweller of the body leaves old bodies and takes on new ones. A question arises here. Just as childhood, youth, and old age come naturally, similarly, the change of bodies also comes naturally (as said in the second chapter, the thirteenth shloka). But here, the words '' and '' seem to be missing. However, the Lord's intention is not to say that the dweller of the body has the freedom to choose its bodies, but rather to remove the sorrow of separation from the body. Just as a person leaves old clothes and takes on new ones, and yet remains the same, similarly, the dweller of the body leaves old bodies and takes on new ones, and yet remains unchanged; therefore, there is no reason to grieve. Another question is that just as leaving old clothes and taking on new ones is a pleasant experience, similarly, leaving old bodies and taking on new ones is a painful experience. Therefore, how can the words '' and '' be applied here? The answer is that the pain of death is not due to death itself, but due to the desire to live. There is a desire to live, 'I want to live', and this desire is the cause of pain. When a person identifies himself with his body, he considers death as his own death and feels pain. But when a person does not identify himself with his body, he does not feel pain at death, but rather joy. Just as a person does not feel pain when changing clothes, because he knows that the clothes are separate from him, similarly, when a person does not identify himself with his body, he does not feel pain at death. The second question is that just as changing clothes is a pleasant experience, similarly, changing bodies is a painful experience. As long as one is aware of the fleeting nature of life, one can see that the body is constantly dying. Just as childhood dies as soon as youth arrives, so too is childhood constantly dying. But because one is not aware of this, one does not see the constant dying of the body. This is what is meant by being in a state of unconsciousness.

and in this shloka (22), Shri Krishna explains that even the doer of actions is crying. This sorrow arises due to ignorance and lack of understanding. To remove this ignorance, the Lord has used the words 'yathaa' and 'tathaa' to give an example of clothes. Here, the Lord has used the word 'grihnaati' (takes) for putting on clothes, but 'sanyati' (goes) for taking on bodies. It may seem that the person remains in one place and puts on clothes, but the body goes to different bodies. The Lord has used this difference in action to explain the worldly view. Special Point
99
However, the body becomes old. Therefore, in childhood, it was the same, and in youth, it is the same. But due to the identification with the body, it attributes the changes in the body to itself. Similarly, the coming and going is the duty of the body, but due to the identification with the body, it thinks that it comes and goes. Therefore, in reality, the body does not come and go anywhere, but due to the identification with the bodies, its coming and going appears. Now, the question arises that what is the reason for the cycle of birth and death that has been going on since time immemorial? From the point of view of actions, it is due to the fruits of good and bad actions that one takes birth and dies. From the point of view of knowledge, it is due to ignorance that one takes birth and dies. In the Gita, it is said, 'Yena sarvam idam tatam' (2.17), 'Nityah hota hai' (2.24), etc., that the body is everywhere and is the cause of birth and death. In all these, the main reason is the eternal, omnipresent, and stable nature of the Supreme Consciousness. The Lord has given the body the freedom to act, and it is due to the misuse of this freedom that one takes birth and dies. Now, the question arises that if the body is everywhere and is the cause of birth and death, how can it be stopped? The answer is that one should use the freedom given by the Lord in a proper way. Therefore, the main reason for the cycle of birth and death is the misuse of the freedom given by the Lord. The solution to this problem is that just as one's respect for one's childhood is the cause of the cycle of birth and death, similarly, one's respect for one's youth is the cause of the cycle of birth and death. When one becomes old, one says, 'I am old.' But in reality, one has not become old; one has just become old in the body. Similarly, when one is young, one says, 'I am young.' But in reality, one has not become young; one has just become young in the body. The real meaning of disrespecting one's knowledge is that one does not act according to what one knows. For example, one knows that telling the truth is good and telling lies is bad, but one tells lies for one's own benefit. One knows that one should not cause pain to others, but one causes pain to others for one's own benefit. Similarly, one knows that the body and other things are not the self, but one identifies with them and feels attachment and aversion towards them. This is the real meaning of disrespecting one's knowledge. Man has a desire for new things, and the Lord also gives him new things. When the body becomes old, the Lord gives him a new body. Therefore, the desire for new things is the cause of the cycle of birth and death. As long as one has a desire for new things, one will get new things. Man has a life force and a desire force. As long as the desire force remains, the life force is destroyed, and one takes birth again. If the desire force is not present, even if the life force is destroyed, one does not take birth again. Any example is only a part of the whole and does not represent the whole. Here, the example of changing old clothes for new ones is only a part of the whole and does not represent the whole. Just as a person remains the same even after changing many clothes, similarly, the self remains the same even after taking many bodies. Just as one does not die by changing old clothes and one does not take birth by putting on new clothes, similarly, one does not die by changing old bodies and one does not take birth by taking new bodies.

Chapter 2, Verse 23

The weapons cannot cut it, nor can the fire burn it. The water cannot wet it, nor can the wind dry it. Explanation:
The weapons cannot cut it - This means that the body cannot be cut by any weapon; because the weapons are made of the earth element, and the earth element cannot cause any disturbance in the body. It is not possible for the earth element to penetrate the body. The fire cannot burn it - This means that the fire cannot burn the body; because the fire is also made of the earth element, and the earth element cannot cause any disturbance in the body. It is not possible for the fire to penetrate the body. The water cannot wet it - This means that the water cannot wet the body; because the water is also made of the earth element, and the earth element cannot cause any disturbance in the body. It is not possible for the water to penetrate the body. The wind cannot dry it - This means that the wind cannot dry the body; because the wind is also made of the earth element, and the earth element cannot cause any disturbance in the body. It is not possible for the wind to penetrate the body. The five elements - earth, water, fire, air, and space - are the five great elements. The Lord has mentioned that the first four elements - earth, water, fire, and air - cannot cause any disturbance in the body. But He has not mentioned the fifth element - space. This is because space has no power to act. The wind cannot dry it - This means that the wind cannot dry the body; because the wind is not able to penetrate the body. The wind is not able to cause any disturbance in the body. The body is eternal and indestructible. The first four elements - earth, water, fire, and air - get their existence from the body. Therefore, how can they cause any disturbance in the body? The body is all-pervading, and the first four elements are pervaded by it. Therefore, how can the pervaded elements cause any harm to the pervader? It is not possible for the pervaded elements to cause any harm to the pervader. In this context, Arjuna is lamenting the death of his relatives. Therefore, the Lord is saying that how can they die? Because the weapons and other instruments of destruction are not able to penetrate the body. Even if the body is cut by a weapon, the body itself is not cut. Even if the body is burned by fire, the body itself is not burned. Even if the body is wet by water, the body itself is not wet. Even if the body is dried by wind, the body itself is not dried.
